entries.summary: Returns the elements sorted using a custom comparator. `comp` should return `true` when its first argument should come before its second.

entries.name: min
entries.summary: Returns the element with the smallest `f` key wrapped in `Just`, or `None` for an empty list.

entries.name: max
entries.summary: Returns the element with the largest `f` key wrapped in `Just`, or `None` for an empty list.

entries.name: sum
entries.summary: Maps each element through `f` and sums the results.

entries.name: join
entries.summary:
Renders and concatenates the elements, placing `sep` between adjacent values. With no separator, the rendered values are joined directly.

Elements do not have to be strings: each is rendered using the same user-facing conversion used by interpolation and printing.

entries.name: Map
entries.summary: Declared for the same reason list.kex declares `type List<X> = [X]`: it gives the name `Map` a source declaration, so it resolves as a type through the collected interfaces rather than needing to be known to the compiler.

entries.name: Map<K, V>
signatures: reduce(acc: A, g: (A -> (K, V) -> A)) -> A
put(k: K, v: V) -> Map<K, V>

entries.name: reduce
signatures: reduce(acc: A, g: (A -> (K, V) -> A)) -> A
entries.summary:
Folds over the map's `(key, value)` pairs in canonical key order.

This is `Map`'s `Enumerable` primitive: `map`, `filter`, `find`, `any?` and the rest are built on it. The block receives the accumulator and one pair; destructure the pair to name its halves.

entries.name: identity
entries.summary: The empty map: the identity element of the `Monoid` instance, so `m.combine({})` is `m`.

entries.name: combine
entries.summary: Combines two maps by merging them, with `other`'s values winning on a key conflict. The `Monoid` operation, and the same thing `merge` does.

entries.name: get
entries.summary:
Returns the value stored under `key`, or `None` when the key is absent.

Missing keys are an ordinary answer rather than a failure, so a lookup on data you did not produce is safe by default. Use the two-argument form below when you have a sensible fallback.

entries.name: put
signatures: put(k: K, v: V) -> Map<K, V>
entries.summary:
Returns a new map with `key` mapped to `value`, replacing any previous entry for that key.

The receiver is untouched. Use `put!` when you want the variable holding the map to be rebound to the result.

entries.name: delete
entries.summary:
Returns a new map without `key`. A key that is not present is not an error: the map comes back unchanged.

Use `delete!` to rebind the receiver variable.

entries.name: has?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when `key` has an entry in the map.

Distinguishes a missing key from one whose value is itself empty, which a `get` with a default cannot.

entries.name: empty?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the map has no entries.

entries.name: count
entries.summary: Returns the number of entries.

entries.name: count
entries.summary: Returns the number of entries satisfying `pred`.

entries.name: keys
entries.summary: Returns the map's keys as a list, in canonical key order.

entries.name: values
entries.summary: Returns the map's values as a list, ordered by their keys.

entries.name: entries
entries.summary:
Returns the map's entries as a list of `(key, value)` tuples, in canonical key order.

This is the bridge to the `List` methods a map does not have of its own, and the form the two-parameter blocks elsewhere are splatting from.

entries.name: each
entries.summary: Calls `f` with each key and value, for its side effects.

entries.name: map
entries.summary:
Applies `f` to each key and value and collects the results into a LIST.

Note the return type: `map` comes from `Enumerable`, whose contract is to produce a list, because `f` may return anything at all. Use `mapValues` or `mapKeys` when you want a map back.

entries.name: mapValues
entries.summary: Returns a new map with every value replaced by `f(value)`. The keys are left alone.

entries.name: mapKeys
entries.summary:
Returns a new map with every key replaced by `f(key)`. The values are left alone.

If `f` maps two keys onto the same result, one entry wins: the map cannot hold both.

entries.name: filter
entries.summary:
Returns a new map with only the entries for which `pred` answers `true`.

Map overrides the map-returning HOFs (Enumerable's default returns a list).

entries.name: reject
entries.summary: Returns a new map with the entries for which `pred` answers `true` removed. The complement of `filter`.

entries.name: merge
entries.summary:
Returns a new map holding the entries of both. When a key appears in both, `other`'s value wins.

The right-biased rule is what makes this the natural way to apply overrides on top of defaults.

entries.name: any?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when at least one entry satisfies `pred`. Stops at the first match.

entries.name: all?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when every entry satisfies `pred`. The empty map answers `true`.

entries.name: find
entries.summary:
Returns the first entry satisfying `pred` as a `(key, value)` tuple, or `None` when nothing matches.

"First" means first in canonical key order.

entries.name: blank?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the map has no entries. The `Blankable` view of `empty?`, so a map can be tested by the same generic code that tests strings and lists.

entries.name: Math
entries.summary:
Mathematical constants and functions.

All trigonometric functions work in radians. Every function here accepts a `Number` (an `Integer` or a `Float`) and the transcendental ones answer with a `Float`.

A Kex `Float` is always finite, so a domain error (`Math.sqrt(-1.0)`) or an overflow (`Math.exp(1000.0)`) raises rather than producing `NaN` or `Infinity`: the same rule the BEAM enforces, where those two values cannot exist at all. There is no non-finite float to test for afterwards.

```kex
Math.sqrt(2.0)              # => 1.4142135623730951
Math.hypot(3.0, 4.0)        # => 5.0
Math.sin(Math.PI / 2.0)     # => 1.0
```

The everyday operations on a single number: `abs`, `floor`, `ceil`, `round`, `sqrt`: are also methods on `Integer` and `Float`, which usually reads better in a chain: `x.abs` over `Math.abs(x)`.

entries.name: PI
entries.summary: The ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter.

entries.name: E
entries.summary: The base of the natural logarithm.

entries.name: sqrt
entries.summary: Returns the square root of `x`. Raises for a negative `x`, which has no real root.

entries.name: cbrt
entries.summary: Returns the cube root of `x`. Unlike `sqrt`, negative input is fine: a negative number has a real cube root.

entries.name: sin
entries.summary: Returns the sine of `x`, given in radians.

entries.name: cos
entries.summary: Returns the cosine of `x`, given in radians.

entries.name: tan
entries.summary: Returns the tangent of `x`, given in radians.

entries.name: asin
entries.summary: Returns the arc sine of `x` in radians, in the range -π/2 to π/2.

entries.name: acos
entries.summary: Returns the arc cosine of `x` in radians, in the range 0 to π.

entries.name: atan
entries.summary:
Returns the arc tangent of `x` in radians, in the range -π/2 to π/2.

Use `atan2` when you have both coordinates of a vector: it can tell the quadrant apart, and this cannot.

entries.name: atan2
entries.summary:
Returns the angle of the vector `(x, y)` in radians, from -π to π.

Both signs are taken into account, so the result lands in the correct quadrant, which is why this, not `atan`, is what you want for converting a vector to an angle. Note the argument order: `y` first.

entries.name: sinh
entries.summary: Returns the hyperbolic sine of `x`.

entries.name: cosh
entries.summary: Returns the hyperbolic cosine of `x`.

entries.name: tanh
entries.summary: Returns the hyperbolic tangent of `x`, always between -1 and 1.

entries.name: log
entries.summary:
Returns the natural logarithm of `x`: its logarithm to base `e`. With a second argument, returns the logarithm to that base instead.

Raises for `x` of zero or less, which has no real logarithm.

entries.name: log2
entries.summary: Returns the base-2 logarithm of `x`. The same as `Math.log(x, 2.0)`, and more direct.

entries.name: log10
entries.summary: Returns the base-10 logarithm of `x`.

entries.name: exp
entries.summary:
Returns `e` raised to the power `x`: the inverse of `Math.log`.

Raises on overflow, which for a double happens a little past `x` of 709.

entries.name: pow
entries.summary:
Returns `x` raised to the power `y`.

The result is always a `Float`, even for whole arguments, so round it when you need an integer back.

entries.name: abs
entries.summary:
Returns the magnitude of `x`, discarding its sign. The type is preserved: an `Integer` in gives an `Integer` out.

`x.abs` is the same thing as a method, and usually reads better.

entries.name: floor
entries.summary: Returns the largest integer that is not greater than `x`: rounding toward negative infinity.

entries.name: ceil
entries.summary: Returns the smallest integer that is not less than `x`: rounding toward positive infinity.

entries.name: hypot
entries.summary: Returns the Euclidean distance +sqrt(x*x + y*y)+, computed so that large values do not overflow on the way.

entries.name: Reader
entries.summary:
Mock: deterministic stand-ins for the world outside the program: the filesystem, environment, and console. Networking mocks live under Mock.Net.

These are STATEFUL: `Mock.FS.File(path, content)` writes into a store the real `FS.File` then reads back, so a test can write and read again, and `clear()` undoes it. That state is global and lives until cleared, which is what makes hook ordering and write/read round trips testable, and also what makes two tests able to interfere.

When a test only needs canned ANSWERS, replacing the capability is the better tool: `with FS.File = MyFake { ... } do ... end` swaps the implementation for one lexical region, holds no global state, needs no clearing, and cannot leak into another test. See spec/capability_stdlib_fs.kex for the shape of a stand-in (kexhq/kex#143).

Opt-in on purpose (issue #144): this module used to ride along inside a prelude networking file, so importing the prelude made every Mock.* reachable from every program without anyone asking for it. Reachable is still not callable: the runtime denies the mock intrinsics outside spec files, the REPL, and --allow-mocks, but it should also not be in scope by accident. A qualified `Mock.FS.File(...)` auto-loads this file like any other opt-in module.

All Mock.* sub-modules live in a single `module Mock` block so merged compilation units never see duplicate top-level `Mock` modules. A stand-in's read hook: a path in, its content or `None` out.

entries.name: Lookup
entries.summary: An environment stand-in's lookup hook: a name in, its value or `None` out.

entries.name: Writer
entries.summary: An environment stand-in's WRITE hook: the name and the value a program set. A `Mock.Env` is an immutable record, so a write cannot land in its `vars`, and it must not reach the real environment, or a test would leak a variable into the next one and into anything the suite starts. The hook is how a test observes the write instead: record it, assert on it, or ignore it, which is what `None` does.

entries.name: Files
entries.summary:
A stand-in for the `FS.File` capability, for `with FS.File = ...`. Unlike the `Mock.*` functions below it holds no global state, needs no `clear()`, and cannot leak past its block. What it cannot do is change: `write` then `read` back is not something a value does, so a test needing that round trip still wants `Mock.FS` (kexhq/kex#143).

```kex
with FS.File = Mock.Files { files: {"kex.toml": "name = \"demo\""} } do
  assert(loadConfig() == "demo")
end
```

`onRead` takes over when a test needs an ANSWER rather than a fixture: content derived from the path, a failure on the third call, a record of what was asked for. It is consulted first and its `None` means "no such file", so a callback can model absence too.

entries.name: Env
entries.summary:
A stand-in for the `ENV` capability. A name simply left out of `vars` reads as unset, which is the whole reason `Mock.ENV.unset` exists: absence is an answer programs act on. `onGet` answers instead of the map when a test wants a rule rather than a fixture.

```kex
with ENV = Mock.Env { vars: {"HOME": "/fake"} } do
  assert(configHome() == "/fake/.config")
end
```

entries.name: Mock.FS
entries.summary:
A stateful stand-in for the filesystem: files a test declares, that the real `FS.File` then reads back.

The store is global and lives until `clear`, which is what makes a write followed by a read testable, and what makes two tests able to interfere. Clear it in an `after` hook.

```kex
describe "the config loader" do
  before do
    Mock.FS.files({ "app.conf": "port = 8080\n" })
  end

  after do
    Mock.FS.clear()
  end

  it "reads the port" do
    Assert.equal(loadPort(), 8080)
  end
end
```

entries.name: File
entries.summary: Declares one file and its content.

entries.name: Directory
entries.summary: Declares a directory at `path`.

entries.name: clear
entries.summary:
Empties the store, so nothing declared so far is visible any more.

Call it in an `after` hook: the store is global, and what one test leaves behind the next one sees.

entries.name: files
entries.summary:
Declares the whole fixture in one call.

The same shape `Mock.Files { files: ... }` takes: one line instead of one per file (kexhq/kex#143).

entries.name: onRead
entries.summary:
Answers reads by RULE rather than from a fixture.

Content derived from the path, a failure on the third call, a record of what was asked for. Consulted before the map, and returning `None` means "no such file", so absence is expressible too.

entries.name: Mock.ENV
entries.summary:
Overlays the process environment, so a test can say what `ENV` holds instead of depending on how it was launched.

The overlay is global and lives until `clear`: clear it in an `after` hook.

```kex
Mock.ENV.vars({ "HOME": "/fake", "LOG_LEVEL": "debug" })
assert(configPath() == "/fake/.config")
Mock.ENV.clear()
```

entries.name: set
entries.summary: Sets one variable in the overlay.

entries.name: unset
entries.summary:
Removes one variable from the overlay, so it reads as unset.

Separate from `set` because a variable being ABSENT is an answer programs act on, and there is no value that means it.

entries.name: clear
entries.summary: Removes the whole overlay, restoring the real environment.

entries.name: vars
entries.summary:
Declares the whole overlay in one call.

The same shape `Mock.Env { vars: ... }` takes (kexhq/kex#143). There is no `onGet` here: global `ENV` is a materialised Map, so there is nothing for a callback to intercept: use `with ENV = Mock.Env { onGet: ... }` when a rule is what you want.

entries.name: Mock.IO
entries.summary:
A stateful stand-in for the console: captures what a program prints, and feeds it lines as if they had been typed.

The way to test a program that talks to a person without one being there.

```kex
Mock.IO.start()
Mock.IO.input("Ada", "42")
greet()
Assert.equal(Mock.IO.output(), "hello, Ada\n")
Mock.IO.stop()
```

entries.name: start
entries.summary: Starts capturing output and serving queued input.

entries.name: stop
entries.summary: Stops capturing, and restores the real console.

entries.name: output
entries.summary:
Everything the program has printed since capturing started.

Newlines are included, so a single `IO.printLine("hi")` gives `"hi\n"`.

entries.name: clear
entries.summary:
Discards the captured output, while continuing to capture.

Useful between phases of one test, when only the later output matters.

entries.name: input
entries.summary:
Queues the lines `IO.getLine` will return, in order.

Takes a list, or up to four lines as separate arguments. Once they run out, `IO.getLine` answers `None`: end of input, exactly as a closed stdin would.

entries.name: cannedRead
entries.summary: Named apart from `read`: `this.read(path)` would bind to the capability's own `read : FilePath -> String?`, not to this method.

entries.name: open
entries.summary: A fake is a value, so there is nowhere for a write to go. Refusing is the honest answer and the useful one: a test that did not expect a write sees it fail rather than silently succeed.

entries.name: lookup
entries.summary: Named apart from `get`: `this.get(key)` would bind to the capability's own `get`, not to this method.

entries.name: set
entries.summary: A write goes to `onSet` or nowhere. It must NOT reach the real environment: a substituted ENV is the whole point of the mock, and a test that set a variable would otherwise leak it into the next one and into every process the suite starts. `vars` cannot take it either: a record is immutable, so a test that cares about writes supplies the hook, and one that does not gets a write that goes quietly nowhere.

entries.name: Mock.Net
entries.summary: Scriptable networking values are namespaced so importing Mock does not recreate any of the removed global HTTP types.

entries.name: Mock.Net.HTTP
entries.summary: Canned HTTP transport state for networking specifications.

entries.name: Transport
entries.summary: Responses returned in order by a scripted transport.

entries.name: Mock.Net.DNS
entries.summary: Canned DNS resolver state for networking specifications.

entries.name: ResolverScript
entries.summary: Hostname-to-address answers supplied without touching the network.

entries.name: Mock.Net.Socket
entries.summary: Canned byte-stream state for socket specifications.

entries.name: Script
entries.summary: Binary chunks delivered in order as incoming socket data.

entries.name: Mock.Net.WebSocket
entries.summary: Canned message state for WebSocket specifications.

entries.name: Script
entries.summary: High-level messages delivered in order by a scripted connection.

entries.name: Net
entries.summary:
Shared networking values, capability discovery, and typed failures.

```kex
using Net

let https = Port.from(443).try
if Support.current.tls.usable? then https.string else "TLS unavailable" end
```

entries.name: Port
entries.summary:
A validated TCP or UDP port number in `0..65535`.

Use `Port.from` at input boundaries. Port zero requests an ephemeral port where a listening API permits it; after binding, ask the server or socket for the concrete port the operating system chose.

entries.name: SupportValue
entries.summary:
Whether a feature was compiled into this backend and is usable now.

`compiled?` describes the build; `usable?` also accounts for the environment it is running in. A browser build may contain an HTTP client, for example, while browser policy still prevents a particular lower-level capability.

entries.name: SupportReport
entries.summary:
Granular networking capabilities for the current backend and environment.

Read this before choosing a transport dynamically. Applications that require one capability can instead check that single field during startup and fail with a useful message.

entries.name: Net.Port
entries.summary: Validated `Port` construction.

entries.name: from
entries.summary: Validates a port number.

entries.name: Net.Support
entries.summary: Runtime discovery for optional network transports and protocols.

entries.name: current
entries.summary: Reports compiled and currently usable networking features.

entries.name: NetOperation
entries.summary: The subsystem or operation that produced a networking error.

entries.name: NetErrorKind
entries.summary: Stable, backend-independent networking failure categories.

entries.name: NetError
entries.summary:
A typed networking failure shared by every network module.

`kind` is the stable category to branch on. `message` is for a person, while `phase` adds protocol context such as a TLS handshake and `progress` records bytes transferred before a partial-operation failure. Keeping those roles separate lets programs recover without matching backend-specific prose.

entries.name: string
entries.summary: Renders the decimal port without a host or scheme.

entries.name: Node
entries.summary:
Distributed Kex: this BEAM node, and the other nodes it is connected to.

A node is one running BEAM VM with a name. Once two nodes share a cookie and are connected, a `Pid` from one works on the other: `send`, `link` and `monitor` cross the network unchanged, and so do typed `Process` and `Server` handles.

Name a node when starting it (`kex --sname a --cookie secret app.kex`), or from inside the program with `Node.start`:

```kex
using Node

main do
  Node.connect(:b@myhost)
  Node.send(:b@myhost, :logger, (:hello, Node.self))
end
```

Node names are atoms: `:b@myhost` for a short name, the quoted `:"b@host.example.com"` for one with dots, or `Atom.from(text)` for one built at runtime.

Both nodes need the same compiled code for anything that carries a function, like a lambda or a record whose methods the receiver calls; `Node.spawn` sends its block's code along. Plain data — numbers, strings, lists, tuples, records — needs nothing.

Backed by Kex.Intrinsic.Node on the BEAM. The tree-walk interpreter is always a single, unnamed node.

entries.name: self
entries.summary: This node's name, or `:nonode@nohost` when it is not distributed.

entries.name: alive?
entries.summary: Whether this node is distributed — started with a name, so other nodes can connect to it.

entries.name: list
entries.summary: The nodes this one is currently connected to, not including itself.

entries.name: start
entries.summary: Makes this node distributed under `name`, as `--sname`/`--name` would at startup. A `name` whose host has a dot (`:"app@host.example.com"`) uses long names; anything else uses short names.

entries.name: stop
entries.summary: Stops distribution: the node drops its name and every connection.

entries.name: connect
entries.summary: Connects to the node named `node`. Both nodes must share a cookie.

entries.name: disconnect
entries.summary: Drops the connection to `node`.

entries.name: setCookie
entries.summary: Sets the cookie this node presents when connecting. Nodes connect only when their cookies match.

entries.name: send
entries.summary: Sends `message` to the process registered as `name` on `node`, unchanged. Like `Pid.send`, it never blocks and never fails.

entries.name: whereIs
entries.summary: The `Pid` registered as `name` on `node`, or `None`.

entries.name: spawn
entries.summary:
Runs `block` in a new process on `node` and returns its `Pid`.

The block is a function of THIS program. When `node` has not loaded the module it belongs to, that module's compiled code is sent over and loaded first. A module `node` already has is left as it is.

entries.name: Integer
entries.summary:
Whole numbers, of arbitrary size.

`Integer` has no width limit: factorials and cryptographic moduli are ordinary values, not a special big-number type you have to opt into.

`Integer` and `Float` are one numeric tower: they compare and order across the boundary, so `0 == 0.0` is `true` and `[1, 2.5, 3].sort` works. What differs is the arithmetic. `/` on two integers is integer division, and `sqrt` answers a `Float` because a square root generally is one.

```kex
7 / 2          # => 3      (integer division)
7.0 / 2.0      # => 3.5
16.sqrt        # => 4.0    (a Float, even from an Integer)
(-7).modulo(3) # => 2      (mathematical modulo, not C remainder)
```

entries.name: even?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the integer is divisible by two. Zero is even, and negative numbers follow the same rule.

entries.name: odd?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the integer is not divisible by two. The opposite of `even?`.

entries.name: abs
entries.summary: Returns the magnitude of the integer, discarding its sign.

entries.name: sqrt
entries.summary:
Returns the square root as a `Float`.

The result is a `Float` even when the root is exact, because in general it is not. Round or floor it when you need an integer back.

entries.name: modulo
entries.summary:
Returns `this` modulo `n`.

The result takes the sign of `n`, which is mathematical modulo rather than the C-style remainder other languages give. That is what makes it safe for wrapping an index that may have gone negative.

entries.name: in?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the integer falls inside `range`, endpoints included.

entries.name: times
entries.summary:
Calls `f` exactly `this` times, passing the 0-based iteration index.

This is the counting loop. When you want the numbers themselves rather than a count of repetitions, `(1..n).items.each` often reads better.

entries.name: floor
entries.summary: Returns the integer unchanged. Present so that code written against `Number` works whichever half of the tower it is handed.

entries.name: ceil
entries.summary: Returns the integer unchanged. The `Integer` counterpart of `Float.ceil`.

entries.name: round
entries.summary: Returns the integer unchanged. The `Integer` counterpart of `Float.round`.

entries.name: Float
entries.summary:
Double-precision floating-point numbers.

A Kex `Float` is always finite. An operation that would produce `NaN` or `Infinity` raises instead: the same rule the BEAM enforces, where those two values cannot exist at all. So a `Float` you are holding is always a real number, and there is no `nan?` to check for.

`Float` and `Integer` compare and order across the boundary; see `Integer` for the rest of the numeric tower.

```kex
3.7.floor      # => 3
3.7.round      # => 4
(-3.7).toInteger  # => -3   (truncates toward zero)
```

entries.name: abs
entries.summary: Returns the magnitude of the float, discarding its sign.

entries.name: sqrt
entries.summary: Returns the square root. Raises for a negative receiver, which has no real root.

entries.name: in?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the float falls inside `range`, endpoints included.

entries.name: floor
entries.summary: Returns the largest integer that is not greater than the float: it always rounds toward negative infinity, which is what separates it from `toInteger` for negative values.

entries.name: ceil
entries.summary: Returns the smallest integer that is not less than the float: it always rounds toward positive infinity.

entries.name: round
entries.summary: Returns the nearest integer, with halves rounding away from zero.

entries.name: toInteger
entries.summary: Truncates toward zero and returns the result as an `Integer`: it drops the fractional part rather than rounding, so it differs from both `floor` and `round` for negative values.

entries.name: Integer
signatures: parse(s: String, radix: Integer) -> Result<Integer, ParseError>
entries.summary:
Reading integers out of text.

Use `parse` when a failure needs explaining and `"42".to(Integer)` when it does not: `to` answers a plain `Optional`, `parse` answers a `Result` carrying a `ParseError` that says where it stopped and what it had read so far.

entries.name: parse
signatures: parse(s: String, radix: Integer) -> Result<Integer, ParseError>
entries.summary:
Parses the whole string as a base-10 integer.

The string must be entirely consumed: leading or trailing characters make it an `Error`, with a `ParseError` describing where parsing stopped. Use `parsePrefix` when a trailing remainder is expected.

entries.name: parsePrefix
entries.summary:
Parses an integer from the front of the string and returns it together with whatever text was left over.

This is the building block for hand-written scanners: parse a number, keep going from the remainder. Answers `None` when the string does not begin with a number at all.

entries.name: Float
entries.summary: Reading floating-point numbers out of text.

entries.name: parse
entries.summary:
Parses the whole string as a float.

The string must be entirely consumed; anything left over makes it an `Error` carrying a `ParseError`.

entries.name: parsePrefix
entries.summary: Parses a float from the front of the string and returns it together with the unconsumed remainder. Answers `None` when the string does not begin with a number.

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary:
The largest finite `Float`.

A Kex `Float` is always finite, so there is no infinity to start from: this is the bound to use instead, say as the first "smallest so far".

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The most negative finite `Float`: `-Float.MAX`. Not the smallest positive one, which some languages call MIN.

entries.name: Float32
entries.summary:
The bounds of the sized numeric types: `Int8.MAX`, `UInt64.MAX`, `Float32.MIN` and so on. `Integer` has none: it is arbitrary-precision. For a float type, `MIN` is the most negative finite value, not the smallest positive one.

The range of a 32-bit float.

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The largest Float32: 3.4028234663852886e38.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The most negative finite Float32: -3.4028234663852886e38.

entries.name: Float64
entries.summary: The range of a 64-bit float, the same as a `Float`.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The most negative finite Float64: -1.7976931348623157e308.

entries.name: Int8
entries.summary: The range of a signed 8-bit integer.

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The largest Int8: 127.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smallest Int8: -128.

entries.name: Int16
entries.summary: The range of a signed 16-bit integer.

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The largest Int16: 32767.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smallest Int16: -32768.

entries.name: Int32
entries.summary: The range of a signed 32-bit integer.

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The largest Int32: 2147483647.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smallest Int32: -2147483648.

entries.name: Int64
entries.summary: The range of a signed 64-bit integer.

entries.name: UInt8
entries.summary: The range of an unsigned 8-bit integer: `UInt8` is another name for `Byte`.

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The largest UInt8: 255.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smallest UInt8: 0.

entries.name: UInt16
entries.summary: The range of an unsigned 16-bit integer.

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The largest UInt16: 65535.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smallest UInt16: 0.

entries.name: UInt32
entries.summary: The range of an unsigned 32-bit integer.

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The largest UInt32: 4294967295.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smallest UInt32: 0.

entries.name: UInt64
entries.summary: The range of an unsigned 64-bit integer.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smallest UInt64: 0.

entries.name: Byte
entries.summary: The range of a `Byte`, Kex's unsigned 8-bit integer (also called `UInt8`).

entries.name: MAX
entries.summary: The largest Byte: 255.

entries.name: MIN
entries.summary: The smallest Byte: 0.

entries.name: Number
entries.summary: Reading a number out of text without deciding in advance which half of the numeric tower it belongs to.

entries.name: parse
entries.summary:
Parses the whole string as an `Integer` or a `Float`, whichever the text describes.

Use it when the input's shape is not known ahead of time: a config value, a CSV column that may hold either.

entries.name: Optional
entries.summary:
An optional value: `Just(x)` carries a value, `None` says there is none.

`X?` is shorthand for `Optional<X>`, and is the spelling you will normally write. Kex has no `null`: anything that might not produce a value returns an `Optional` instead, so the compiler makes you say what happens when it is empty. Most of the time that is a single `.or(default)` at the end of a chain.

Pattern matching handles the cases that need more than a default:

entries.name: Result
entries.summary:
The outcome of an operation that can fail: `Ok(x)` on success, `Error(e)` on failure with a reason.

Use `Result` over `Optional` when the *reason* for failure matters to the caller. Parsing is the standard example: `"12x".to(Integer)` answers `None`, while `Integer.parse("12x")` answers an `Error` that says where it stopped.

entries.name: Either
entries.summary:
One of two values, of possibly different types: `Left(l)` or `Right(r)`.

Unlike `Result`, neither side means failure: `Either` is for a value that is legitimately one of two shapes.

entries.name: Optionable
entries.summary:
A value that may be absent. Constrain a generic parameter with it when a function accepts any optional value.

The two operations below are what make the constraint worth having: an empty trait would accept a value and then let you do nothing with it, since there would be no method to call. `map` is deliberately NOT required — its result type differs per implementer (`Y?` here, `Result<Y, E>` for `Resultable`), which needs a higher-kinded parameter Kex does not have.

entries.name: set?
entries.summary:
Answers `true` when a value is present.

The one operation an `Optionable` type must define; `none?` is its negation.

entries.name: or
entries.summary:
Returns the wrapped value, or `default` when there is none.

The way out of the optional world, and the reason a constrained parameter is usable at all.

entries.name: Resultable
entries.summary: A value that either succeeded or failed with a reason. Constrain a generic parameter with it when a function accepts any result value.

entries.name: ok?
entries.summary:
Answers `true` for a success.

The one operation a `Resultable` type must define; `error?` is its negation.

entries.name: or
entries.summary: Returns the success value, or `default` on failure.

entries.name: Eitherable
entries.summary: One of two values, neither meaning failure. Constrain a generic parameter with it when a function accepts any either value.

entries.name: either
entries.summary:
Case analysis: applies `onLeft` to a `Left` and `onRight` to a `Right`.

The one operation an `Eitherable` type must define — `left?` and `right?` are both written in terms of it. A discriminator alone would let you ask which side a value is on without being able to reach it, which is why this is the requirement rather than those.

entries.name: set?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when a value is present.

entries.name: none?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when there is no value. The opposite of `set?`.

entries.name: or
entries.summary:
Returns the wrapped value, or `default` when there is none.

This is the usual way an optional leaves the optional world: put `.or` at the end of a chain and the rest of your code works with a plain value.

entries.name: map
entries.summary: Applies `f` to the wrapped value, keeping the result wrapped. `None` is returned unchanged, so `f` never sees a missing value.

entries.name: flatMap
entries.summary:
Applies `f`, which itself returns an optional, and flattens the result.

Use it instead of `map` when the step can also fail: `map` would give you a doubly wrapped `Just(Just(x))`, `flatMap` gives a single layer. A `None` anywhere in the chain short-circuits the rest.

entries.name: ok?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the result is `Ok`.

entries.name: error?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the result is `Error`. The opposite of `ok?`.

entries.name: or
entries.summary:
Returns the `Ok` value, or `default` when the result is an `Error`.

The error payload is discarded. Match on the result instead when you need to report why it failed.

entries.name: map
entries.summary: Applies `f` to the `Ok` value. An `Error` passes through untouched, so a chain of `map` calls describes the success path only.

entries.name: flatMap
entries.summary:
Applies `f`, which itself returns a `Result`, and flattens the result.

The step-by-step form of `map` for stages that can fail on their own. The first `Error` ends the chain and is the answer.

entries.name: optional
entries.summary:
Converts the result to an `Optional`, dropping the error payload.

Useful when a caller only needs to know whether there is a value, and everything downstream already speaks `Optional`.

entries.name: to
signatures: to(value, t: Type, radix: Integer) -> A?
entries.summary:
Converts `value` to the type `t`, or `None` if it cannot be represented.

`t` is a runtime type value: write the type name itself: `String`, `Integer`, `Float`, `List`. Conversion to `String` goes through the `Showable` protocol, so it works for every value.

The result is an `Optional`, not a `Result`, and deliberately so: the reason a conversion failed is usually implied by the types alone. When the reason carries information (where a parse gave up and on what) reach for `Integer.parse` or `Float.parse`, which answer with `Result<_, ParseError>`. So: `to` for every day, `parse` when the failure needs handling.

entries.name: either
entries.summary:
Case analysis: applies `onLeft` to a `Left` and `onRight` to a `Right`.

The way an `Either` is consumed without a `match`, and the operation `Eitherable` requires. Both branches answer the same type, so the result is a plain value rather than another `Either`.

entries.name: left?
entries.summary: Returns `true` for a `Left`.

entries.name: right?
entries.summary: Returns `true` for a `Right`. The opposite of `left?`.

entries.name: OptionKind
entries.summary: What kind of value an option carries: `StringValue` takes any text, `IntegerValue` must parse as a number, and `FlagValue` takes none at all and reads as `"true"` when present.

entries.name: OptionSpec
entries.summary: One declared option. Built for you by the `OptionConfig` builders: you rarely construct one by hand.

entries.name: CommandHandler
entries.summary: What a command does once the line has been parsed. It receives the parsed options with the command's own words already removed, so `tey add greet` hands its handler `["greet"]`, and returns the process exit code.

entries.name: CommandSpec
entries.summary: One declared command. Built for you by the `OptionConfig.command` builders.

entries.name: OptionConfig
entries.summary:
A tool's whole command-line interface: its name, its options, and its commands.

Build one with `OptionParser.define` and add to it with the chainable `string`, `integer`, `flag` and `command` methods. Each returns a new `OptionConfig`, so the chain reads as one declaration.

entries.name: ParsedOptions
entries.summary: The result of a successful parse: the option values, and the words that were not options.

entries.name: OptionParseError
entries.summary:
Why a command line could not be parsed.

`OptionParser.errorMessage` turns one into a sentence for the user; `OptionConfig.run` does that for you.

entries.name: value
entries.summary: Returns the value given for the option named `name`, or `None` when it was neither supplied nor defaulted.

entries.name: flagEnabled?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the flag named `name` was given.

entries.name: integerValue
entries.summary:
Returns the value of an integer option as an `Integer`, or `None` when it is absent or does not parse.

An option declared with `integer` has already been checked at parse time, so `None` here means absent rather than malformed.

entries.name: OptionConfig
signatures: string(long: String, short: Char?, description: String, default: String?, required?: Bool) -> OptionConfig
integer(long: String, short: Char?, description: String, default: String?, required?: Bool) -> OptionConfig
flag(long: String, short: Char?, description: String) -> OptionConfig
command(name: String, usage: String, description: String, section: String, handler: CommandHandler) -> OptionConfig
passthroughCommand(name: String, usage: String, description: String, handler: CommandHandler) -> OptionConfig

entries.name: string
signatures: string(long: String, short: Char?, description: String, default: String?, required?: Bool) -> OptionConfig
entries.summary: Declares an option that takes a text value.

entries.name: integer
signatures: integer(long: String, short: Char?, description: String, default: String?, required?: Bool) -> OptionConfig
entries.summary:
Declares an option that takes a whole number.

A value that does not parse is rejected at parse time with `InvalidInteger`, so a handler never sees a malformed number. Read it back with `ParsedOptions.integerValue`.

entries.name: flag
signatures: flag(long: String, short: Char?, description: String) -> OptionConfig
entries.summary:
Declares an option that takes no value and is either present or not.

It defaults to `"false"` and reads as `"true"` when given. Read it back with `ParsedOptions.flagEnabled?`. Giving it a value is an error (`UnexpectedValue`).

Declare a flag named `help` if you want `--help` to print the help text: `run` looks for exactly that name, and adds nothing on its own.

entries.name: command
signatures: command(name: String, usage: String, description: String, section: String, handler: CommandHandler) -> OptionConfig
entries.summary:
Declares a command and the function that runs it.

A command name may be several words (`"docs build"`) and the longest match wins, so a group and its subcommands can both be declared. The handler receives the parsed options with the command's own words already removed, and returns the process exit code.

Declares a command. `usage` is what the help line shows after the name (`<name>`, `[args...]`); leave it empty for a command that takes none.

entries.name: passthroughCommand
signatures: passthroughCommand(name: String, usage: String, description: String, handler: CommandHandler) -> OptionConfig
entries.summary:
Declares a command that parses its own options.

Everything after the command's name is handed to the handler in `arguments` untouched, including options this tool also declares. Use it for a subcommand backed by its own `OptionConfig`: without it, an option the outer tool happens to declare too is consumed here and never reaches the subcommand, with no error to say so.

entries.name: parse
entries.summary:
Parses `args` into option values and leftover words, without dispatching to a command.

Use it when the tool has no commands, or when you want to inspect the parse before deciding what to do. `run` is the one-call alternative.

entries.name: run
entries.summary:
Parses `args`, runs the command they name, and returns its exit code.

This is the whole of a tool's `main`: hand it the argument list and pass the result to `System.exit`.

A parse failure, an unknown command, or a line with no command at all reports the problem along with the help text and returns 1: the one place that policy has to live for every tool to behave the same way. A set `help` flag prints the help and returns 0.

entries.name: printHelp
entries.summary:
Prints the help text and returns 0, the exit code for a successful run.

`run` calls this for you when the `help` flag is set; call it directly when a tool decides on its own that help is the right answer.

entries.name: help
entries.summary:
Returns the tool's help text: its name and description, its options, and its commands grouped by section.

`run` and `printHelp` print this for you; reach for it directly when the text has to go somewhere other than stdout.

The help text, styled. Every escape comes from `Console`, which the runtime blanks under `--no-colors` and `KEX_COLORS=0`, so the same code produces plain text down a pipe and this needs no second rendering path.

Widths are measured on the UNSTYLED label throughout: an escape sequence has a length that a terminal does not draw, so padding computed from a coloured string lines the columns up on paper and nowhere else.

entries.name: define
entries.summary:
Starts an immutable command-line interface definition.

Chain options and commands onto the returned `OptionConfig`, then call `parse` with the process arguments. `name` appears in usage text and `description` introduces the generated help page.

entries.name: commandLabel
entries.summary: Returns the label a command is listed under in the help text: its name, followed by its usage when it has one.

entries.name: commandFor
entries.summary:
Finds the declared command whose words open `arguments`, and returns it with whatever is left after them.

Longest match first, so `"kex install"` is preferred over a `"kex"` that also exists. Answers `None` when no command matches.

entries.name: passthrough?
entries.summary:
Whether the command `arguments` names parses its own options.

`false` when no command matches yet, so options before any command word are still this parser's to claim.

entries.name: opensWith?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when `arguments` begins with the words of `name`.

The word-wise prefix test `commandFor` matches with: `"docs build"` opens `["docs", "build", "src"]` but not `["docs"]`.

entries.name: errorMessage
entries.summary:
Renders a parse error as a sentence for the user.

`OptionConfig.run` does this for you; call it directly when handling a `parse` result yourself.

entries.name: parse
entries.summary:
Parses `args` against a list of option and command specs.

The engine behind `OptionConfig.parse`, which is the form to call from ordinary code.

entries.name: Parsing
signatures: some(f: (Input -> Result<(T, Input), ParseError>)) -> Result<([T], Input), ParseError>
choice(alts: ([(Input) -> Result<(T, Input), ParseError>])) -> Result<(T, Input), ParseError>
entries.summary:
Parser combinators, for reading a text format you define yourself.

Opt-in: nothing here is in scope until `using Parsing`.

An `Input` is an immutable cursor over a string. A parser takes one and answers either the value it read together with an advanced cursor, or a `ParseError` saying where it gave up. Because the cursor is immutable, a failed attempt costs nothing: the caller still holds the position it started from and can try something else.

```kex
using Parsing

main do
  let cursor = Input { input: "abc 123" }
  let word = cursor.takeWhile(~alpha?)
  let (text, rest) = word
  IO.printLine(text)              # prints: abc
  IO.printLine(rest.pos)          # prints: 3
end
```

The building blocks are `char` and `charWhen` for one character, `string` for a literal, `takeWhile` for a run, and `many` / `some` / `choice` for repetition and alternatives. `JSON` in this same stdlib is written with them.

entries.name: ParseError
entries.summary:
Why a parser gave up, and at which position.

`Expected` carries what the grammar WANTED rather than what it found: the difference between "unexpected `d`" and "expected `version(`". It is what `label` and `string` report.

```kex
Input { input: "abc" }.char('z')      # => Error(Unexpected("a", 0))
Input { input: "abc" }.string("abd")  # => Error(Expected("abd", 0))
```

entries.name: Input
entries.summary:
An immutable cursor over a string: the text, and where in it you are.

Create one with `Input { input: text }` and pass it to a parser. Every operation that consumes input answers a NEW cursor rather than moving this one, which is what makes backtracking free.

entries.name: Input
signatures: some(f: (Input -> Result<(T, Input), ParseError>)) -> Result<([T], Input), ParseError>
choice(alts: ([(Input) -> Result<(T, Input), ParseError>])) -> Result<(T, Input), ParseError>

entries.name: peek
entries.summary:
The character at the cursor, or `None` at the end of the input.

Looking does not consume: the cursor is unchanged.

entries.name: peekAt
entries.summary:
The character `offset` positions ahead of the cursor, or `None` when that is outside the input.

The lookahead a grammar needs when one character is not enough to decide. A negative offset looks backwards.

entries.name: atEnd?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when the cursor has consumed the whole input.

The check a top-level parser makes at the end, to be sure nothing was left over.

entries.name: advance
entries.summary: A cursor one character further on.

entries.name: advanceBy
entries.summary: A cursor `count` characters further on.

entries.name: remaining
entries.summary:
Everything from the cursor to the end of the input, as a `String`.

Useful for reporting an error, or for handing the tail to something that does not speak `Input`.

entries.name: charWhen
entries.summary:
Reads one character, if it satisfies `pred`.

Answers the character and the advanced cursor, or an `Unexpected` error naming what was there instead: `"EOF"` at the end of the input.

entries.name: char
entries.summary: Reads one specific character.

entries.name: whiteSpaces
entries.summary:
A cursor advanced past any run of whitespace.

Cannot fail: no whitespace at all leaves the cursor where it was, which is what makes it safe to call between every token of a grammar.

entries.name: many
entries.summary:
Applies `f` as many times as it succeeds, collecting the results.

Cannot fail: zero matches is an empty list, which is what makes it right for the optional parts of a grammar. A parser that succeeds without consuming anything stops the loop rather than spinning forever.

entries.name: some
signatures: some(f: (Input -> Result<(T, Input), ParseError>)) -> Result<([T], Input), ParseError>
entries.summary:
Applies `f` at least once, then as many more times as it succeeds.

The one-or-more counterpart of `many`: the first failure IS a failure, so use it where the grammar requires something to be there.

entries.name: string
entries.summary:
Reads an exact literal.

A keyword grammar is mostly literals: `version(` is one token to a reader and eight calls to `char`, and matching it here reports the failure at the START of the literal, which is where a person looking at the error expects the caret.

entries.name: takeWhile
entries.summary:
Reads every character while `pred` holds, as a `String`.

`many(charWhen(...))` gives a [Char] the caller has to join, and a run of characters is almost always wanted as text. Cannot fail: an empty run is an empty String, which is what makes it safe for the optional parts of a grammar.

entries.name: choice
signatures: choice(alts: ([(Input) -> Result<(T, Input), ParseError>])) -> Result<(T, Input), ParseError>
entries.summary:
Tries each parser in `alts` in turn, and answers the first that succeeds.

This is alternation: how a grammar says "a value is a string, or a number, or an object". Because the cursor is immutable, a failed alternative costs nothing. When none of them match, the answer is `NoMatch` at the position they all started from.

entries.name: Pid
entries.summary:
An opaque BEAM process identifier.

Obtained from `Process.self` or `Process.whereIs`. Send it messages, link to it, monitor it, or ask whether it is still alive.

entries.name: Task
entries.summary:
A handle on work running in another process, with a result you can await.

Created by `Task.start`.

entries.name: Reference
entries.summary: A monitor reference, returned by `monitor` and passed back to `demonitor`.

entries.name: Process
entries.summary: A typed process handle: like a `Pid`, but it remembers what kind of message the process accepts.

entries.name: ProcessExitReason
entries.summary: A process termination reason. This remains open because the BEAM permits any term as an exit reason; conventional values include `:normal`, `:shutdown`, and structured application errors.

entries.name: Reply
entries.summary:
What a synchronous `slot` returns: an answer for the caller, and optionally a new state and a reason to stop.

`reply` answers the caller immediately. A slot may omit it only when it sends a deferred response with `from.reply(...)`. `new` installs the next serving state; omitting it preserves the current state. `stop` terminates the server after applying the transition. Within a `serving X` block, the checker narrows `new` from `Any?` to `X?`.

```kex
slot allowed? -> Reply<Bool> do
  let allowed = @remaining > 0
  new.remaining = allowed then @remaining - 1 else @remaining
  return { new, reply: allowed }
end

slot stop -> Reply<Integer> = { stop: :normal, reply: @remaining }
```

entries.name: From
entries.summary: The identity of a pending caller, for a slot that answers later rather than immediately. Hand it `reply` when the answer is ready.

entries.name: CallError
entries.summary: Why a call into a server failed: it took too long, the process is gone, or it crashed handling the call.

entries.name: Server
entries.summary:
A running server and the default timeout for calls into it.

Returned by `Process.spawn`. Every `slot` declared in the type's `serving` block becomes a method on it, answering a `Result`.

entries.name: Process
signatures: run(command: String, args: [String]) -> Integer -> Result<ProcessResult, String>
entries.summary: Spawning servers, running external commands, and the ambient process operations.

entries.name: spawn
entries.summary:
Starts a process running the `serving` implementation attached to `state`'s type, and returns a handle on it.

The state you pass is the server's initial state. Every `slot` in the `serving` block becomes a method on the returned `Server`, and each answers a `Result`: a call can time out or find the process gone.

entries.name: run
signatures: run(command: String, args: [String]) -> Integer -> Result<ProcessResult, String>
entries.summary:
Runs an executable with an argument vector and captures its output.

No shell is involved, so nothing is glob-expanded or word-split and arguments containing spaces need no quoting. Output is captured as UTF-8 strings.

A non-zero exit status is still `Ok`: the program ran and said something, which is information, not a failure to run it. `Error` means the child could not be started at all.

entries.name: stream
entries.summary:
Runs an executable with the CALLER's stdout and stderr, so its output appears as it is produced rather than in one block when it exits.

Answers the exit code; nothing is captured: that is the trade, and it is what a long-running child a person is watching needs (kexhq/kex#187).

`run` remains the one to use when the output is data to be READ.

entries.name: exec
entries.summary:
Runs an executable and returns just its exit code, discarding its output.

A command that could not be started answers `127`, the shell's convention for "command not found". Use `run` when you need the output or want to tell a failed start from a failed run.

entries.name: self
entries.summary: Returns the calling process's own `Pid`.

entries.name: exit
entries.summary:
Sends an exit signal carrying `reason` to `pid`.

`:normal` is the ordinary shutdown reason; `:kill` cannot be trapped.

entries.name: register
entries.summary: Registers `pid` under the atom `name`, so it can be found by name rather than by passing the `Pid` around.

entries.name: whereIs
entries.summary: Returns the `Pid` registered under `name`, or `None` when nothing is.

entries.name: Shared
entries.summary:
A named, typed slot of state that every process can read without asking another process for it.

State kept in a `serving` process is copied into the caller on every read, which is costly for a large value read by every request. A `Shared` value is stored once for the whole node (on the BEAM, in `persistent_term`): reading it copies nothing, however large it is.

The price is on the other side: replacing a value makes the runtime scan every process for references to the old one. So it suits state that is read constantly and written rarely, such as configuration or a loaded site, and not a counter.

Get a handle with `Process.Shared.named`. The slot is identified by its name alone, so two handles with the same name are the same slot; the type parameter is what a handle promises to store and read back, so give every handle on one name the same one.

entries.name: named
entries.summary: The handle on the slot called `name`. Nothing is stored or read until `put` or `get`.

entries.name: put
entries.summary:
Stores `value`, replacing whatever the slot held.

Expensive: see `Process.Shared`.

entries.name: get
entries.summary:
The stored value, or `None` when nothing has been stored yet.

Cheap, whatever the value's size.

entries.name: delete
entries.summary: Empties the slot.

entries.name: ProcessResult
entries.summary:
What an external command left behind: its exit status and its output.

Returned inside `Ok` by `Process.run`, whatever the exit status.

entries.name: send
entries.summary:
Sends `msg` to the process, unchanged, as a raw BEAM term.

Sending never blocks and never fails, even when the process is gone: that is the BEAM's model, not an oversight. Monitor the process when delivery matters.

entries.name: sendFrom
entries.summary: Sends the conventional Erlang sender-bearing pair `{Process.self, msg}`, so the receiver knows where to answer.

entries.name: link
entries.summary:
Links the calling process to this one, so that either one exiting abnormally takes the other down.

Linking is bidirectional and is how a group of processes is made to fail together. Use `monitor` when you want to be told about a death without sharing it.

entries.name: unlink
entries.summary: Removes the link between the calling process and this one.

entries.name: monitor
entries.summary:
Starts monitoring this process, and returns the reference that identifies the monitor.

When the monitored process exits, the caller receives a message about it. Unlike `link`, a monitor is one-directional and does not propagate the exit. Pass the reference to `demonitor` to stop.

entries.name: alive?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when the process is still running.

Inherently a snapshot: the process may exit immediately after you ask. Monitor it when the answer has to stay true.

entries.name: Process<X>
entries.summary: A spawned Process<X> is a typed process handle backed by the same runtime pid. It therefore supports the ordinary pid lifecycle operations without erasing its message type.

entries.name: send
entries.summary: Sends `msg` to the process. Unlike `Pid.send`, the message type is checked.

entries.name: sendFrom
entries.summary: Sends the sender-bearing pair `{Process.self, msg}`, with the message type checked.

entries.name: link
entries.summary: Links the calling process to this one. See `Pid.link`.

entries.name: unlink
entries.summary: Removes the link between the calling process and this one.

entries.name: monitor
entries.summary: Starts monitoring this process. See `Pid.monitor`.

entries.name: alive?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the process is still running.

entries.name: within
entries.summary:
Returns the same server with a different default call timeout, in milliseconds.

The server is untouched: this is a new view of it, so one slow call can be given more room without changing anything for other callers.

entries.name: link
entries.summary: Links the calling process to the server. See `Pid.link`.

entries.name: unlink
entries.summary: Removes the link between the calling process and the server.

entries.name: monitor
entries.summary: Starts monitoring the server. See `Pid.monitor`.

entries.name: alive?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the server is still running.

entries.name: reply
entries.summary:
Answers the pending call this value identifies.

A slot that cannot answer immediately, because it is waiting on something else: omits `reply` from its transition and calls this later instead.

entries.name: pid
entries.summary: Returns the waiting caller's `Pid`.

entries.name: Task
entries.summary: Running work in another process and collecting the answer.

entries.name: sleep
entries.summary: Suspends for an elapsed duration. Negative durations are treated as zero.

entries.name: start
entries.summary:
Runs `f` in a new process and returns a handle on its result.

The block starts immediately, so starting several tasks and awaiting them afterwards is what makes them run at the same time.

entries.name: awaitAll
entries.summary:
Waits for every task in `tasks` and returns their results, in the order the tasks were given.

Each result comes back wrapped in a `Result`, so one task failing does not cost you the others' answers. That differs from `Task.await` on a single task, which hands back the value itself.

entries.name: await
entries.summary: Waits for the task's result, for as long as it takes.

entries.name: await
entries.summary:
Waits for the task's result, giving up after `timeout` milliseconds.

Answers `None` if the task has not finished in time. The task itself is not stopped.

entries.name: worker
entries.summary: Wraps a spawn block into a worker spec for `Supervisor.start`.

entries.name: demonitor
entries.summary: Stops the monitor this reference identifies.

entries.name: Random
entries.summary:
Random values for simulations, sampling, games, and reproducible tests.

Import with `using Random`. Ordinary calls return a value directly; a `Random.Generator` returns `(value, nextGenerator)`. Reusing the same generator replays the same draw. Pass its returned state to continue.

These generators are not cryptographic; do not use their output for secrets. `Random.secureBytes` and `Random.token` are, and are what secrets come from.

entries.name: Generator
entries.summary:
Immutable state of a deterministic random sequence.

Construct with `Random.seeded` or `Random.fresh`. Each draw returns its value first and the advanced generator second. Equal seeds reproduce equal sequences for the same operations on both backends.

entries.name: seeded
entries.summary: Starts a deterministic sequence. Any Integer seed is reduced modulo 2^64.

entries.name: fresh
entries.summary: Starts a generator using fresh host entropy.

entries.name: integer
entries.summary: Draws an integer between both endpoints, with the advanced generator. The range must be ascending and contain at most 2^64 integers. A singleton range is valid and still consumes a draw.

entries.name: float
entries.summary: Draws a float from the lower bound inclusive to the upper bound exclusive. Defaults to `0.0..1.0`. Bounds must be finite and strictly ascending.

entries.name: boolean
entries.summary: Draws a fair Boolean and returns the advanced generator.

entries.name: chance?
entries.summary: Draws true with the supplied probability. Consumes one draw even at 0 or 1.

entries.name: choice
entries.summary: Chooses an input position uniformly. Empty input returns None without a draw.

entries.name: sample
entries.summary: Selects input positions without replacement, in random order. Duplicate input values may appear more than once in the result. A count larger than the input selects every position; zero consumes no draws.

entries.name: shuffle
entries.summary: Returns a random permutation, preserving duplicates and the input itself. Empty input consumes no draws.

entries.name: integer
entries.summary: Draws an integer from an inclusive range using fresh entropy.

entries.name: float
entries.summary: Draws a float; defaults to [0.0, 1.0). The upper bound is excluded.

entries.name: boolean
entries.summary: Draws a fair coin flip using fresh entropy.

entries.name: chance?
entries.summary: Returns true with the supplied probability using fresh entropy.

entries.name: choice
entries.summary: Chooses a position uniformly, returning None for an empty input.

entries.name: sample
entries.summary: Samples positions without replacement; duplicate values remain possible.

entries.name: shuffle
entries.summary: Returns a random permutation using fresh entropy.

entries.name: secureBytes
entries.summary:
Returns `count` bytes from the operating system's cryptographically secure generator: the source for keys, session tokens and unguessable identifiers, which the generators above must never be used for.

Nothing about it is reproducible, and there is no `Generator` form.

entries.name: token
entries.summary: Returns an unguessable token: `bytes` secure random bytes, as lowercase hex, so the text is twice as long as `bytes`.

entries.name: Range
entries.summary:
A span between two bounds, written `(1..10)` or `('a'..'z')`.

A range stores its endpoints on both backends without building a list. Integer and character ranges can be enumerated with both ends included. Float ranges describe continuous bounds, for example `(-1.0..1.0)` for random sampling; they cannot be enumerated without an explicit step.

```kex
(1..5).items          # => [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
(1..5).sum            # => 15
5.in?(1..10)          # => true
('a'..'e').items      # => ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e']
```

It is `Enumerable` and `Foldable`, so the traversal methods work directly, and the list operations below answer in list terms. Use `items` when you want a real list to hand to something else.

```kex
(1..10).items.filter(~even?)   # => [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
(1..3).items.each { |n| IO.printLine(n) }
```

entries.name: Range
signatures: reduce(acc: A, f: (A -> B -> A)) -> A

entries.name: reduce
signatures: reduce(acc: A, f: (A -> B -> A)) -> A
entries.summary:
Folds over the range's elements in ascending order.

This is `Range`'s `Enumerable` primitive; the traversal methods are built on it. A range stays structurally minimal, so the fold runs over its materialized items.

entries.name: sum
entries.summary: Returns the sum of the range's elements.

entries.name: product
entries.summary: Returns the product of the range's elements.

entries.name: contains?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when `value` falls inside the range, endpoints included.

`5.in?(1..10)` says the same thing from the value's side, and often reads better.

entries.name: items
entries.summary:
Returns the range's elements as a list.

This is where a range stops being two numbers and becomes real data, so it is also where a very large range starts to cost something.

entries.name: first
entries.summary:
Returns the first element, or `None` for an empty range.

The list operations, over the materialized items. A range is an ordered collection, so `(1..5).first` and `(1..5).length` operate on its materialized elements. Floating bounds do not define such a collection.

entries.name: second
entries.summary: Returns the second element, or `None` when the range is shorter than two.

entries.name: third
entries.summary: Returns the third element, or `None` when the range is shorter than three.

entries.name: last
entries.summary: Returns the last element, or `None` for an empty range.

entries.name: rest
entries.summary: Returns every element after the first, as a list.

entries.name: length
entries.summary: Returns how many elements the range has.

entries.name: count
entries.summary: Returns how many elements the range has. The same as `length`.

entries.name: empty?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the range has no elements.

entries.name: max
entries.summary: Returns the largest element, or `None` for an empty range.

entries.name: min
entries.summary: Returns the smallest element, or `None` for an empty range.

entries.name: reverse
entries.summary: Returns the elements as a list, in descending order.

entries.name: sort
entries.summary: Returns the elements as a sorted list. A range is already ascending, so this is the identity: it exists so that generic code can call it.

entries.name: sort
entries.summary: Returns the elements as a list, ordered by `comparator`.

entries.name: uniq
entries.summary: Returns the elements as a list with duplicates removed. A range has none, so this is the identity: it exists so that generic code can call it.

entries.name: join
entries.summary: Renders the elements as text, with `separator` between them.

entries.name: at
entries.summary:
Returns the element at index `index`, counting from 0, or `None` when out of range.

Note that the index counts positions, not values: `(10..20).at(0)` is `Just(10)`.

entries.name: get
entries.summary: Returns the element at index `index`, counting from 0, or `None` when out of range. The same as `at`, named to match `List` and `Map`.

entries.name: take
entries.summary: Returns the first `n` elements as a list.

entries.name: drop
entries.summary: Returns everything after the first `n` elements, as a list.

entries.name: indexOf
entries.summary: Returns the position of `value` in the range, or `None` when it is not in it.

entries.name: zip
entries.summary: Pairs each element with the element at the same position in `other`, stopping at the shorter of the two.

entries.name: partition
entries.summary: Splits the elements into those satisfying `pred` and those that do not.

entries.name: push
entries.summary: Returns the elements as a list with `value` added at the end.

entries.name: reject
entries.summary: Returns the elements that do NOT satisfy `pred`, as a list.

entries.name: Regex
signatures: get(key: Atom | Integer, default: String) -> String
replace : String -> Regex -> String | (Match) -> String -> String

entries.name: Regex
entries.summary:
Regular expressions, backed by PCRE2 in the interpreter and Erlang's `re` on BEAM: the same PCRE pattern language on both.

Opt-in, not prelude: nothing here is in scope until `using Regex`.

There are two ways to write a pattern. The tagged literal is the everyday one: it is checked when your program is compiled, so it cannot fail at run time and gives you a bare `Regex`.

```kex
using Regex

main do
  let line = "order #4271 shipped"
  IO.printLine(line.matches?(re`#\d+`))                     # => true
  IO.printLine(line.matches(re`#(\d+)`).map { |m| m.get(1) })  # => 4271
end
```

The call form takes a pattern built at run time and answers a `Result`, because an arbitrary string may not be a valid pattern:

```kex
match regex(userSupplied) do
  Ok(pattern) => IO.printLine(text.matches?(pattern))
  Error(e)    => IO.printError("bad pattern at ${e.position}: ${e.message}")
end
```

The operations are `matches?` (is it there), `matches` (find the first), `scan` (find them all), `replace`, and `split`.

A compiled regular expression.

`Regex` carries only its pattern source. The compiled engine object lives in a runtime cache keyed by that source, deliberately: a compiled pattern bakes in the host's PCRE version and must never be embedded in a distributed artifact, so the source string is the value's identity.

entries.name: RegexError
entries.summary:
A pattern that failed to compile.

Mirrors `ParseError`: the `position` is a *character* offset into the pattern, not a byte offset, so it agrees across backends on patterns containing non-ASCII.

```kex
regex("(")
# => Error(RegexError { source: "(", position: 1,
#                       message: "missing closing parenthesis" })
```

entries.name: regex
entries.summary:
NOTE: deliberately does NOT `implement: Errorable`, even though the trait exists for exactly this shape. Declaring a `message` method alongside the `message` field makes `e.message` dispatch to the method instead of reading the field, which fails with `undef` on the BEAM backend. `ParseError`: the prelude's equivalent error record: carries a bare `message` field for the same reason; nothing in the tree implements Errorable today.

Compiles `source` into a `Regex`.

Answers a `Result` because an arbitrary string may not be a valid pattern. Use this form when the pattern is built at run time: from a config file, from user input. For a pattern you write yourself, the tag form `` regex`\d+` `` is checked at compile time and hands back a bare `Regex`.

entries.name: validateRegex
entries.summary:
Validates a `regex` tagged literal at compile time.

Found by the compiler through the standard `validate<Tag>` naming convention (nothing about regex is special-cased). A raw `` regex`(` `` is a compile error, with the caret pointing at the byte offset PCRE2 reported inside the literal.

Must stay pure: the compiler evaluates it on the tree-walk interpreter at compile time, so marking it `foul` would break builds, not just calls.

entries.name: re
entries.summary:
A short alias for `regex`, in both its forms.

A second name bound to the same two functions, not a lexer synonym, so every property of `regex` (escaping, backend mapping, error shape) applies to it unchanged. Most code uses the tag form, where the shorter name reads better.

entries.name: validateRe
entries.summary: Validates an `re` tagged literal at compile time, delegating to `validateRegex`. The compiler finds it by the same `validate<Tag>` convention.

entries.name: quote
entries.summary:
Escapes every regex metacharacter in `s`, so the result matches `s` literally.

This is how to search for text that may itself contain pattern syntax: a search term typed by a user, a filename, a version string. It escapes per character rather than wrapping in `\Q...\E`, which a value containing `\E` would break out of.

entries.name: Match
entries.summary:
A successful match, and the groups it captured.

It behaves like a map keyed by both group number (`0` is the whole match) and group name (`:year`), but is a named type so it can grow spans and surrounding context later without breaking existing `get` call sites.

A group that did not participate is an absent key, so `get` answers `None`. This differs from a group that matched the empty string, which answers `Just("")`.

entries.name: Match
signatures: get(key: Atom | Integer, default: String) -> String
entries.summary: NOTE: the accessor is `get`, not `get`. A `make` block on a user type that defines a method name the prelude also uses breaks that name's dispatch for every OTHER type on the BEAM backend: with `get` here, merely saying `using Regex` made a plain `someMap.get(k)` fail with function_clause. `get` also matches Python's `m.get(1)` and Java's `matcher.get(1)`. A plain Map's `get` is unaffected: resolution picks a local method by receiver type, name and arity.

entries.name: get
signatures: get(key: Atom | Integer, default: String) -> String
entries.summary:
Returns the text captured by a group, by number or by name.

Group `0` is the whole match; `1` is the first parenthesised group. A named group `(?<year>...)` is reached with the atom `:year`. A group that did not participate answers `None`.

entries.name: matches
entries.summary:
Finds the first occurrence of `re` in `s` and returns what it matched.

Unanchored: the pattern may match anywhere in the string. Anchor it with `^...$` when a whole-string match is what you mean. Answers `None` when the pattern does not occur.

entries.name: matches?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when `re` occurs anywhere in `s`.

The boolean form of `matches`, and unanchored for the same reason. Use it when you only need to know whether the pattern is there.

entries.name: scan
entries.summary:
Returns every match of `re` in `s`, left to right.

Always answers `[Match]`, whether or not the pattern has capture groups: adding a group to a pattern must not change the type flowing out of `scan`. An empty list means nothing matched.

entries.name: replace
signatures: replace : String -> Regex -> String | (Match) -> String -> String
entries.summary:
Replaces EVERY match of `re` in `s`: this is `gsub`, not `sub`.

The replacement is either a literal `String`, inserted verbatim with no `$1` / `\1` backreference syntax, or a block receiving the `Match`, which is how a replacement built from what was captured is written.

entries.name: splitLimit
entries.summary:
Splits `s` on `re`, capping the number of fields.

A positive `limit` caps the field count, leaving the remainder unsplit in the last field; a negative `limit` keeps trailing empty fields instead of dropping them.

Plain `s.split(re)` needs no function here at all: it resolves to `String.split`, which dispatches to this engine when handed a Regex (in both backends), and follows Ruby's semantics: trailing empty fields are dropped, leading ones are kept, and capture groups are interleaved into the result.

Only the limit form needs a name, and it deliberately is NOT `split`: this module must not export that name. On BEAM, a module in scope via `using` captures a method name for EVERY receiver, so exporting `split` here would route `"a,b".split(",")` and even the no-argument `"hi".split` through this module and break them.

entries.name: Stream
entries.summary:
A lazy, potentially infinite sequence.

A stream describes how to produce its elements rather than holding them, so an infinite one is an ordinary value. Nothing is computed until you ask for elements with `take`.

```kex
let naturals = Stream.Sequence(from: 0) { |n| n + 1 }
naturals.take(5)                              # => [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
naturals.map { |n| n * n }.take(4)            # => [0, 1, 4, 9]
naturals.filter { |n| n.even? }.take(3)       # => [0, 2, 4]
```

`map`, `filter` and `drop` all answer with another stream, so a pipeline stays lazy end to end; `take` is what turns it into a list.

Streams are best for generated sequences you may revisit. A file or socket is different: it can only be consumed once, so those APIs return a `Feed`. Convert a small feed with `toStream` only when replaying it is worth keeping every value already read.

entries.name: Stream
entries.summary: Constructors for `Stream`.

entries.name: Sequence
entries.summary:
Builds an infinite stream from a first element and a step function.

The stream is `from`, then `step(from)`, then `step(step(from))`, and so on: nothing is computed until you take from it.

entries.name: Iterate
entries.summary: Builds an infinite stream from a seed and a step function. The same thing as `Sequence`: use whichever reads better where you are.

entries.name: empty
entries.summary: The stream with no elements.

entries.name: take
entries.summary:
Returns the first `n` elements as a list, computing the stream up to that point.

This is the operation that ends a lazy pipeline and gives you real data.

entries.name: drop
entries.summary:
Returns a new stream that skips the first `n` elements.

Still a stream, so the result stays lazy: pair it with `take` to get a window out of the middle.

entries.name: map
entries.summary:
Returns a new stream with `f` applied to each element.

`f` is not called until elements are taken, and then only for those that are.

entries.name: filter
entries.summary:
Returns a new stream with only the elements `pred` accepts.

Producing `n` filtered elements may require walking many more upstream ones, so a predicate that almost never holds makes `take` run for a long time, and one that never holds makes it run forever.

entries.name: each
entries.summary:
Applies `f` to every element.

Only ever finishes on a stream that ends: a file's lines converted with `Feed.toStream`, or anything `take` has bounded. On `Stream.Sequence` this runs forever, exactly as writing the same loop by hand would.

entries.name: toFeed
entries.summary:
Returns a `Feed` that walks this stream once.

A stream remembers every element forced through it, so walking a long one holds all of it for as long as the stream is in scope. A feed drawn from it walks without holding the start, letting each element go as it passes: the way to consume a long stream in constant space.

entries.name: String
signatures: reduce(acc: A, f: (A -> Char -> A)) -> A
entries.summary:
Text. A `String` is a sequence of Unicode characters, immutable like every other Kex value: every method here answers with a new string rather than changing the receiver.

A `String` is its own type, not a list of characters. It is `Enumerable`, so `each`, `reduce`, `find` and friends walk it one `Char` at a time, and the sequence operations that could reasonably answer in either currency pick the useful one: `take`, `drop` and `sort` hand back a `String`, while `first` and `last` hand back a `Char`. Use `chars` to cross over to a real list.

```kex
let line = "  Hello, World  "
line.trim.lowerCase.split(", ")   # => ["hello", "world"]
line.trim.take(5)                 # => "Hello"
line.trim.chars.count(~upper?)    # => 2
```

Strings interpolate with `${...}`:

```kex
let name = "Ada"
"hello, ${name}"                  # => "hello, Ada"
```

entries.name: reduce
signatures: reduce(acc: A, f: (A -> Char -> A)) -> A
entries.summary:
