entries.summary:
A declaration, expression, pattern or type, holding its own tokens and nested nodes in source order.

```kex
let tree = Kex.AST.parseSyntax("# the answer\nlet x = 42\n").try
tree.kind                  # => "Program"
Kex.AST.toSource(tree)     # => "# the answer\nlet x = 42\n"
```

entries.name: parseSyntax
entries.summary: Parses Kex source into its lossless syntax tree.

entries.name: toSource
entries.summary:
Reprints a syntax tree as the source it was parsed from, byte for byte.

Every node prints its own tokens and its nested nodes in order, never a slice of the original text, so a rearranged tree prints the rearranged program, its comments moving with it.

entries.name: elementSource
entries.summary: The source of one child of a node: a token's trivia and text, or a nested node reprinted.

entries.name: commentsBefore
entries.summary:
The comments written on their own lines directly above the child at `index`: the ones that belong to it, move with it when a formatter moves it, and hold a `# kex:disable-next-line` meant for it.

A comment at the end of the previous line trails that line instead, and is not included.

entries.name: blankLinesBefore
entries.summary:
How many blank lines separate the child at `index` from what precedes it.

Kept as a count, not a flag: a formatter preserves one blank line between declarations and collapses longer runs, which needs to know how many there were.

entries.name: linesBefore
entries.summary: The whole lines between the child at `index` and the code before it, as the trivia of the `Newline` tokens that end them. The newline that ends the previous line of code is not one of them: what sits in front of it trails that code.

entries.name: TypeRef
entries.summary:
A type as it was written in source.

`typeRefText` renders one back to the source spelling.

entries.name: typeRefText
entries.summary:
Renders a `TypeRef` back to the way it is written in source.

A list reads as `[Integer]`, a map as `{String: Integer}`, an optional as `String?`: the spelling a reader would recognise, not the constructor tree behind it.

entries.name: PatternRef
entries.summary:
Structured representation of patterns.

Pattern nodes describe what a declaration or match arm accepts; they do not contain runtime values. A linter can distinguish a wildcard from a binding, for example, without reparsing source text.

entries.name: PatternField
entries.summary:
One field inside a record or map-shaped pattern.

`pattern` is `None` for shorthand such as `{ name }`. `stringKey` keeps `{"name": value}` distinct from the atom-key spelling `{ name: value }`.

entries.name: patternRefText
entries.summary: Renders a `PatternRef` back to the way it is written in source.

entries.name: referenceText
entries.summary:
Renders either a type or a pattern back to source.

The one call to reach for when a node may carry either: it dispatches to `typeRefText` or `patternRefText` as appropriate.

entries.name: Expression
entries.summary:
Structured representation of expression AST nodes.

Expressions retain syntax-level distinctions that matter to tools: a method call is not flattened into a generic call, `var` is distinct from `let`, and a trailing `if` remains recognizable. Walk these constructors when writing a linter or code search; use `Evaluator` when the goal is to execute an expression rather than inspect it.

entries.name: NamedArgument
entries.summary: One `name: value` argument at a call site.

entries.name: MatchArm
entries.summary:
One arm of `match`, `receive`, or `rescue`.

Multiple `patterns` are the comma-separated alternatives on the left of the arrow. `guard` is absent when the arm has no `when` condition.

entries.name: LambdaParam
entries.summary: One lambda parameter and its optional source annotation.

entries.name: RescueInfo
entries.summary:
The structured recovery clauses attached to a function or expression.

Named rescue arms live in `arms`; a catch-all rescue keeps its optional binding and body separately. `inlineReturn` represents the compact rescue form rather than inventing a synthetic block.

entries.name: ElseIf
entries.summary: One `elif` branch, in source order.

entries.name: MapItem
entries.summary: One entry in a map literal: either a key/value pair or `...spread`.

entries.name: RecordField
entries.summary: One explicitly initialized field in a record literal.

entries.name: GeneratedTemplate
entries.summary:
A declaration template whose name (and, for a make block, target) is computed by a `compiled do` expression.

Tools normally encounter this only while inspecting metaprogramming code. After expansion, generated declarations appear as ordinary +Node+s.

entries.name: GeneratedMakeInfo
entries.summary: The fixed portion of a generated `make` declaration.

entries.name: MainInfo
entries.summary: The program entry point, including documentation and recovery clauses.

entries.name: ParamInfo
entries.summary:
One declared function parameter.

`name` is absent for a destructuring parameter; `pattern` preserves that destructuring shape. `hasDefault` records whether an initializer appeared.

entries.name: ClauseInfo
entries.summary:
One clause of a function, including its patterns and body.

Multi-clause functions place all clauses in one `FunctionInfo`, preserving source order so tooling can reason about which pattern is tried first.

entries.name: FunctionInfo
entries.summary:
A named function and all of its pattern-matching clauses.

`doc` contains the normalized `#` comment immediately attached to the declaration. Documentation generators can therefore share the same parsed structure as linters instead of scanning comments independently.

entries.name: AnnotationInfo
entries.summary:
A standalone function or method type signature.

`implicitThis` distinguishes `:>` methods from module-level `:` functions without making a tool inspect punctuation in the original source.

entries.name: VariantInfo
entries.summary: One constructor of an algebraic data type.

entries.name: TypeInfo
entries.summary:
A type alias or algebraic data type declaration.

`variants` is present for an ADT and absent for an alias or abstract type. `parents` preserves declared bounds and inherited type relationships.

entries.name: FieldInfo
entries.summary: One field declared by a record type.

entries.name: RecordInfo
entries.summary: A record declaration with fields in source order.

entries.name: TraitInfo
entries.summary: A trait declaration and the signatures or default methods in its body.

entries.name: MakeInfo
entries.summary:
A `make` implementation block.

`target` is the receiver type, `implements` lists explicit traits, and `body` retains methods and visibility sections in declaration order.

entries.name: PragmaInfo
entries.summary: A compiler pragma and its optional value.

entries.name: ModuleInfo
entries.summary: A module and its declarations in source order.

entries.name: ConstantInfo
entries.summary: A named constant declaration. The AST reader never evaluates its value.

entries.name: VisibilityInfo
entries.summary: A `public` or `private` section and the declarations it contains.

entries.name: UsingInfo
entries.summary: A `using` import, including aliasing, filters, and an optional scoped body.

entries.name: ExportInfo
entries.summary: An `export` declaration and its public-name filters.

entries.name: CompiledItem
entries.summary: One item inside a `compiled do` block before expansion.

entries.name: CompiledInfo
entries.summary: A compile-time block and its declarations or expressions in source order.

entries.name: Node
entries.summary:
Any top-level or declaration-level AST node.

A source tool can match only the declarations it understands and leave the rest alone. The program's `schemaVersion` lets persisted consumers reject a tree whose possible node shapes have changed.

entries.name: TypeRef | PatternRef
entries.summary:
Source-like conversion through the standard `to(String)` spelling.

Useful in diagnostics: a tool can interpolate the type or pattern it found without manually dispatching between the two reference families.

entries.name: Net.DNS
signatures: lookup(kind: RecordType, name: Name) -> Result<LookupResponse, NetError>
entries.summary:
Typed DNS lookup with explicit resolver ownership and bounded caching.

Use `DNS.addresses` for an occasional hostname lookup. Own a `Resolver` when a service performs repeated lookups, needs cache statistics, or must query a particular nameserver. Resolver ownership makes both caching and cleanup visible instead of hiding process-wide state behind every lookup.

```kex
using Net.DNS

let resolver = Resolver.system.try
let name = Name.parse("example.test").try
let addresses = resolver.addresses(name).try
resolver.close
```

entries.name: Name
entries.summary:
A validated DNS name with caller-facing and IDNA ASCII spellings.

`display` keeps the readable form supplied by the caller; `ascii` is the wire-safe IDNA form used in DNS queries. Keeping both lets an error message say what the user typed without sending noncanonical labels to a resolver.

entries.name: RecordType
entries.summary: Record families supported by `Resolver.lookup`.

entries.name: DNSSECStatus
entries.summary: DNSSEC state reported by the underlying resolver. Kex does not independently validate DNSSEC and therefore commonly reports `Indeterminate`.

entries.name: DNSRecord
entries.summary: Typed DNS resource records, preserving MX/SRV priorities and TXT chunks.

entries.name: LookupResponse
entries.summary: Records and the reported DNSSEC state from one lookup.

entries.name: CacheOptions
entries.summary:
Bounds for a resolver-owned positive and negative cache.

Positive answers honor their DNS TTL up to `maximumTtl`. Failed lookups are cached for `negativeTtl`, preventing a missing hostname from hammering the configured nameserver on every request.

entries.name: Nameserver
entries.summary: One DNS server used by a custom resolver.

entries.name: ResolverOptions
entries.summary: Isolated resolver configuration. An empty search list only queries the name as written; search domains are tried in order for single-label names.

entries.name: CacheStatistics
entries.summary:
Lifetime cache counters. `clear` empties entries but keeps these counters.

Compare `hits` with `misses` when tuning `entries` or TTL bounds. A rising `evictions` count means the resolver is seeing more distinct names than its cache can retain.

entries.name: Resolver
entries.summary: An opaque, process-safe resolver that owns its cache.

entries.name: Net.DNS.Name
entries.summary: Validation and IDNA conversion for DNS names.

entries.name: parse
entries.summary: Validates a name and converts Unicode labels to IDNA ASCII.

entries.name: Net.DNS.Resolver
entries.summary: Constructors for long-lived, cache-owning resolvers.

entries.name: system
entries.summary:
Opens a resolver using system configuration and default cache bounds.

Reuse the returned resolver for the lifetime of a service so repeated names benefit from its bounded cache, then close it during shutdown.

entries.name: custom
entries.summary:
Opens an isolated resolver with typed nameservers and query bounds.

This does not inherit the machine's search domains or nameservers. It is useful for tests, service discovery, and applications with their own DNS policy.

entries.name: Resolver
signatures: lookup(kind: RecordType, name: Name) -> Result<LookupResponse, NetError>

entries.name: addresses
entries.summary:
Resolves AAAA and A records, returning IPv6 addresses first.

This is the convenient operation for connecting to a host. Use `lookup` when record type, TTL-related behavior, or DNSSEC status matters.

entries.name: lookup
signatures: lookup(kind: RecordType, name: Name) -> Result<LookupResponse, NetError>
entries.summary: Looks up one supported resource-record family.

entries.name: clear
entries.summary:
Empties cached entries without resetting lifetime counters.

Existing statistics remain meaningful across a manual refresh, while the next lookup is forced back to DNS.

entries.name: statistics
entries.summary: Reports current occupancy and lifetime cache counters.

entries.name: close
entries.summary:
Idempotently closes the resolver.

Calls after closing fail with `Closed`; closing again is harmless.

entries.name: Net.DNS.DNS
entries.summary: Convenience lookup operations for callers that do not need resolver ownership or cache reuse.

entries.name: addresses
entries.summary:
Resolves a name once with a short-lived system resolver.

Prefer this for command-line tools and one-off checks. A server that looks up names repeatedly should own a `Resolver` so it can reuse cached answers.

entries.summary:
Buffered HTTP clients, responses, and a small declaration-ordered server router. Requests never follow redirects or perform generic retries implicitly.

```kex
using Net.HTTP

let response = HTTP.get("https://example.test/").try
response.status.success?   # => true
```

For connection reuse and statistics, own a client explicitly:

```kex
let client = Client.open.try
let response = client.get("https://example.test/").try
client.close.try
```

entries.name: Headers
entries.summary:
An insertion-ordered HTTP field collection. Names compare case-insensitively and duplicate fields are preserved.

A list of pairs rather than a `{String: String}` map, and deliberately so. A map cannot hold the same name twice, and `Set-Cookie` needs exactly that: RFC 6265 does not define it as a comma-separated list, so two cookies must travel as two fields and cannot be joined into one. A map interface would read as the obvious one right up to the first response that sets two cookies, then silently keep one — the same class of quiet data loss this module's `Result`-returning builders exist to avoid.

Order is kept for the same reason. RFC 9110 makes order insignificant BETWEEN different names but significant between fields sharing a name, and a map has no order to keep.

entries.name: Status
entries.summary: A validated HTTP status code in `100..599`.

entries.name: Response
entries.summary: A typed HTTP response envelope whose body representation is explicit.

entries.name: Request

entries.summary: Route captures decoded after path segmentation.

entries.name: Context
entries.summary: Per-request server context.

entries.name: Handler
entries.summary: A buffered HTTP route handler. Handling a request is effectful: routes may read files, query a database, send messages, or perform other application IO.

entries.summary: One declared route; routers preserve declaration order.

entries.summary: An immutable, declaration-ordered HTTP router.

entries.summary: Counts and elapsed time from graceful server shutdown.

entries.name: ServerOptions
entries.summary: Bounded HTTP server resources and default graceful-shutdown duration.

entries.name: PoolOptions

entries.name: Client
entries.summary: The pooled HTTP client. An opaque handle over the connection pool that owns it; `Client.open` makes one and `client.close` releases it.

Duplicate fields stay in their original order. Invalid names and values containing line breaks are rejected instead of creating a malformed or injectable HTTP message.

Use this at a protocol boundary when headers arrive as text. Application code normally builds them with `from`, `add`, and `set`.

entries.summary: Validates an HTTP status code.

Use this for a method without a convenience function. Paths may include named or wildcard captures, which the handler reads from `RouteContext`.

entries.name: start
signatures: start(endpoint: Net.Socket.TCP.Endpoint, router: Router, options: ServerOptions) -> Result<Running, NetError>
entries.summary:
Starts a server with conservative defaults and returns immediately.

The returned handle owns the listener and active handlers. Use `start` when the process has other work to do; use `serve` for a foreground server whose main job is handling HTTP.

entries.summary:
Appends a field, keeping existing fields of the same name.

Repeats are how `Set-Cookie` works: it is not a comma-separated list, so two cookies must be two fields. For replace-semantics, `remove` first.

An invalid name or value is an `Error`, not a silent drop. entries.name: Net.IP
entries.summary:
Validated, canonical IP addresses and CIDR networks.

```kex
using Net.IP

let address = Address.parse("192.0.2.42").try
let network = Network.parse("192.0.2.0/24").try
network.contains(address)   # => true
```

entries.name: Address
entries.summary:
A canonical IPv4 or IPv6 address.

The stored spelling is normalized, so addresses that arrived in different forms compare and print consistently. Zone identifiers such as `%en0` are properties of socket endpoints and do not belong here.

entries.name: Network
entries.summary:
A canonical CIDR network with host bits cleared.

Parsing `192.0.2.9/24` therefore produces `192.0.2.0/24`. This makes a `Network` suitable for access-control rules and routing tables: its identity is the range, not whichever host address happened to describe it.

entries.name: Net.IP.Address
entries.summary: Strict parsing and canonicalization of individual IP addresses.

entries.name: parse
entries.summary: Parses IPv4 or IPv6 text and canonicalizes its spelling.

entries.name: Net.IP.Network
entries.summary: Strict parsing and canonicalization of CIDR networks.

entries.name: parse
entries.summary: Parses a CIDR and clears host bits.

entries.name: string
entries.summary: Returns the canonical text form of the address.

entries.name: version
entries.summary: Returns the address family as `4` or `6`.

entries.name: loopback?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` for an address that routes back to this host.

This covers the IPv4 `127.0.0.0/8` block as well as IPv6 `::1`; it is not limited to the familiar `127.0.0.1` spelling.

entries.name: private?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` for an address reserved for private networks.

Use this as one signal in a network policy, not as proof that a peer is trusted: private addresses can still belong to another machine.

entries.name: unspecified?
entries.summary:
Returns `true` for the all-zero address: `0.0.0.0` or `::`.

On a listening endpoint this usually means "all local interfaces". It is not a usable remote destination.

entries.name: multicast?
entries.summary: Returns `true` when the address names a multicast group.

entries.name: string
entries.summary: Returns canonical CIDR text, including the prefix length.

entries.name: contains
entries.summary:
Returns `true` when `address` falls within this network.

An address from the other family is simply outside the network; callers do not need to compare `version` first.

entries.name: prefix
entries.summary: Returns the number of fixed leading address bits.

entries.name: first
entries.summary: Returns the first address in the range: the address with all host bits cleared.

entries.name: last
entries.summary:
Returns the last address in the range: the address with all host bits set.

This is the IPv4 broadcast-shaped endpoint of the mathematical range; the API does not decide whether a protocol permits assigning it to a host.

entries.name: Net.HTTP.WebSocket
signatures: connect(url: String, options: ClientOptions) -> Result<Connection, NetError>
entries.summary:
High-level RFC 6455 client messages. The runtime handles fragmentation and ping/pong frames; reconnect and heartbeat policies remain application-owned.

A `Connection` delivers complete messages rather than wire frames. Your code never has to assemble fragments or answer a protocol ping, but it does decide what a dropped connection means: reconnecting may require resubscribing or replaying an application cursor, so the library cannot do that safely for you.

```kex
using Net.HTTP.WebSocket

let socket = WebSocket.connect("wss://example.test/events").try
socket.send(Text("hello")).try
let message = socket.receiveMessage.try
socket.close
```

entries.name: Message
entries.summary:
A complete high-level WebSocket message. Fragmentation and ping/pong control frames are handled by the connection runtime.

`CloseMessage` carries the peer's status code and reason. Treat it as the end of the message stream even when the code describes a normal shutdown.

entries.name: ClientOptions
entries.summary:
Client handshake policy and the maximum reassembled message size.

Subprotocols are offered in preference order. The byte limit applies after fragments are reassembled, preventing a peer from bypassing the bound with many individually small frames.

entries.name: Session
entries.summary: Negotiated handshake information. The subprotocol is `None` when the server selected none.

entries.name: Connection
entries.summary: An opaque RFC 6455 connection, client- or server-side. It does not reconnect automatically.

entries.name: Handshake
entries.summary: Subprotocols offered by an incoming upgrade request, in the order the peer listed them.

entries.name: Upgrade
entries.summary:
A server's decision after inspecting a `Handshake`.

`Accept` takes over the connection once the 101 response is sent: `handler` runs with the negotiated server `Connection`, and its return value is discarded. `headers` are added to the 101 response; a name that manages the handshake itself (`Upgrade`, `Connection`, `Sec-WebSocket-Accept`, `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`) is dropped rather than overridden. `subprotocol` must be one `handshake.subprotocols` actually offered, or `None`.

`Reject` answers with an ordinary buffered response instead, leaving the connection as plain HTTP — a client requesting an unsupported subprotocol might get `Response.text(426, "chat.v2 required")`, for instance.

A `CloseMessage` is returned once so the application can inspect the peer's reason. Subsequent reads fail with `Closed`.

entries.name: Units.Data
signatures: convertTo(measure: Measure, unit: DataUnit) -> Result<Measure, String>

entries.summary:
Data sizes: bytes, kilobytes, and their binary counterparts.

Opt-in: nothing here is in scope until `using Units.Data`.

```kex
using Units.Data

main do
  IO.printLine(1500.megabytes.to(String))              # prints: 1500.0 MB
  IO.printLine(1500000000.byteSize.to(String, in: Giga)) # prints: 1.5 GB
end
```

Both families are here and they are not the same: `KB` is 1000 bytes, `KiB` is 1024. Values built from either convert freely, because both are counted in bytes underneath, so `1.gibibytes.convertTo(MiB)` answers 1024 MiB.

Every value is a `Measure` from the prelude, so its arithmetic, comparison and `to(String)` apply unchanged.

entries.name: DataUnit
entries.summary:
The data units this module names: decimal (`KB`, `MB`, `GB`, `TB`) and binary (`KiB`, `MiB`, `GiB`, `TiB`), plus the plain byte `B`.

```kex
1.KB   # 1000 bytes
1.KiB  # 1024 bytes
```

entries.name: DataPrefix
entries.summary:
A decimal prefix to render a size at: `Kilo` means KB, `Mega` means MB, `Giga` means GB.

entries.name: Units.SI
entries.summary:
SI units: metres, grams, watts, volts and the rest, with prefixes and dimensional arithmetic.

Opt-in: nothing here is in scope until `using Units.SI`.

```kex
using Units.SI

main do
  IO.printLine(3.kilo.watt.to(String))          # prints: 3000.0 W
  IO.printLine(5000.meter.kilo.to(String))      # prints: 5.0 km
  IO.printLine((100.meter / 10.sec).to(String)) # prints: 10.0 m/s
end
```

Every value is a `Measure` from the prelude, so the arithmetic, conversion and comparison described there apply unchanged. What this module adds is the SI vocabulary, the prefixes, and a table of which dimension results from multiplying or dividing two others, so `2.newton * 3.meter` answers in joules and `100.meter / 10.sec` in metres per second.

```kex

```

entries.summary: Include the source URL in the cache identity: two packages with the same display name must never share a checkout.

entries.name: parser
entries.summary:
Options AND commands in one declaration: OptionParser matches the command words, strips them, and hands the handler what is left. Tey keeps no dispatcher of its own, so the help text and what actually runs cannot drift apart — they are read off the same list.

`foul` because the handlers do things.

entries.name: cli
entries.summary:
The parser Tey actually runs: the declared commands, plus one for every `command(...)` this package's manifest declares. Registering them here rather than in a fallback is what gets them into `tey help`, into the unknown-command message, and into argument stripping, for free.

A package command can never shadow a built-in: the manifest reader refuses those names outright (Tey.Manifest.reservedCommands). They are listed under their own help heading regardless — "unknown command" should send a reader to package.kex or to Tey, and the two lists are written by different people.

entries.name: dispatch
entries.summary: The line is parsed once here to answer the two questions `run` cannot — is this `--version`, and does it name a command Tey already answers — and then handed to `run`, which parses it again and dispatches. A parse ERROR is left to `run` as well: reporting it with the help text is the one policy every tool built on OptionParser shares.

entries.name: announceToolchain
entries.summary:
Tells the rest of the process which compiler Tey selected.

`Kex.AST` — which is how a `package.kex` is read at all — shells out to the compiler named by `$KEX`, falling back to whatever `kex` PATH happens to hold. Tey is started by `erl`, not by `kex`, so nothing had set that: a manifest was parsed by an unrelated compiler if one was on PATH, and by none at all otherwise — which is why a package's commands silently vanished from `tey help` on a machine where `kex` was installed only inside the Tey home.

An explicit `$KEX` is left alone: someone who set it means it, and that is the documented override the compiler itself honours.

entries.summary: `tey install <argument>`: a program, from a path for now. A Git URL and an installed program's name (reinstalling it) are the next steps of docs/plan_tey_global_install.md.

entries.name: installFromPath
signatures: installFromPath(path: String, packageName: String, force?: Bool) -> Integer
entries.summary: Installs the program at `path` without touching it: the workspace around it is copied into a staging directory, which gets its own lock, dependencies and build, and only replaces the program's previous build tree once its programs are in place. The user's checkout gains no `ebin/`, no `tey.lock`, nothing.

entries.name: programMember
signatures: programMember(context: Context, packageName: String) -> Result<Member, String>
entries.summary: The member of `context` a path install means: the one `--package` names, else the one the path is inside of.

entries.name: installStaged
signatures: installStaged(context: Context, member: Member, staging: String, force?: Bool) -> Integer

entries.name: dependencyClosure
entries.summary: Names affected by a member-local or named update, including transitive dependency edges recorded in the newly resolved graph.

entries.name: mergeUpdate
signatures: mergeUpdate(previous: LockState, fresh: LockState, roots: [String], wholeWorkspace?: Bool) -> LockState
entries.summary: Publishes fresh workspace metadata and selected resolutions while retaining unrelated external pins. Existing approvals are carried forward here and subsequently filtered against the visible declarations by approvePlugins.

entries.name: lockReusable?
signatures: lockReusable?(state: LockState, manifestFingerprint: String, toolchain: Tey.Toolchain.ToolchainInfo) -> Bool

entries.name: installTargetsSelected
signatures: installTargetsSelected(context: Context, packageName: String, force?: Bool = …) -> Integer

entries.name: installMemberTargets
entries.summary:
Puts this package's `target(...)` executables where they can be run by name, and records them in the package's receipt (see Tey.Programs).

`${TEY_HOME}/bin` is a directory Tey already owns and already asks people to put on PATH — it is how the `kex` shim gets there — so a package's programs land beside it rather than needing a second directory and a second instruction.

Only packages that DECLARE a target are affected. A library has none, so `tey install` in one still means exactly what it meant before: fetch the dependencies.

Every name is checked before anything is built, so a refused install costs nothing and changes nothing.

entries.name: installMemberTargetsFrom
signatures: installMemberTargetsFrom(member: Member, force?: Bool, origin: Receipt) -> Integer
entries.summary: `installMemberTargets`, recording `origin`'s source fields in the receipt — a program built in a staging copy came from somewhere else.

entries.name: releaseTarget
signatures: releaseTarget(owner: String, name: String) -> Result<Void, String>
entries.summary: Drops `name` from `owner`'s receipt after another package took it over with `--force`; a receipt left owning nothing is removed.

entries.name: recordInstall
signatures: recordInstall(package: ManifestPackage, origin: Receipt, installed: [String], receipts: [Receipt], claims: [(String, Claim)]) -> Result<Void, String>
entries.summary: Writes the package's receipt and settles ownership around it: names taken over with `--force` leave the other package's receipt, and targets the previous receipt owned that this install no longer declares are removed from the bin directory rather than left behind unowned.

entries.name: dependencyRoots
entries.summary: `--source-root` for every fetched dependency. Without these a dependency is just bytes in the cache: `using Greet` cannot find it, and the package that declared it does not compile. A dependency the lockfile names but the cache does not have is reported rather than quietly dropped — the answer is `tey install`, and silence would look like a broken `using`.

entries.name: dependencyRootsAt
entries.summary: `dependencyRoots` for the workspace around `start` rather than around the working directory. A program being installed from a path is built in a staged copy while the user stands somewhere else entirely — possibly in another project, whose lockfile would otherwise supply the dependencies.

entries.name: sourceRoots
entries.summary: Every `--source-root` a compile of THIS package needs: its own `src/` first, then each dependency's. Own-first is deliberate — a package that shadows a dependency's module name means its own, the same way `--source-root` order already decides that for dependencies among themselves.

entries.name: librarySources
entries.summary: A library's compilable units: every `.kex` directly under `src/`. Not a recursive walk — a nested module is reached by the file that declares it, and compiling it twice by name is how you get a duplicate-module error out of a perfectly good package.

entries.name: librarySourcesAt
entries.summary: Returns units relative to `packageRoot`, not absolute: the compiler double-registers a module's declarations when the entry file it is asked to compile is an absolute path that also falls under an explicit `--source-root` (kexhq/kex#?, surfaced by `tey build`ing Rodolfo — a `private do` function building a record literal of a type carrying earlier `make` methods reported that type's method "defined twice"). A relative unit, resolved through the working directory `streamAt`/`runAt` `cd` into, does not collide with the source-root the same way. Callers must invoke the compiler with `packageRoot` as the working directory.

entries.name: backendFlags
entries.summary:
What `tey build` produces is what ships, so what `tey run` and `tey test` exercise has to be the same thing — which is what `kex` does with no backend flag at all: it compiles and runs on the BEAM. `-R` tree-walks the source instead, and processes, `BEAM.*` interop and the String/Char representation differ enough between the two that a green interpreter run says nothing about the built package.

`--interpret` is the way back, for a backend gap or a debugging session.

entries.name: runPackage
signatures: runPackage(extra: [String], interpret?: Bool, packageName: String = …) -> Integer

entries.name: runCommand
signatures: runCommand(command: Command, extra: [String], interpret?: Bool) -> Integer
entries.summary:
`tey <name>` for a `command(...)` the manifest declares.

A `.kex` script is run through the SELECTED toolchain with this package's source roots already in place — the same environment `tey run` gives, so a release script can `using` the package it is releasing. Anything else is a shell line: `sh -c` is what makes `command("fmt", run: "kex --format src")` behave the way the same line behaves in a terminal, pipes and `&&` included. Trailing arguments are passed as "$@" rather than pasted into the string, so `tey fmt --check` cannot be re-split by the shell.

The `--` before the arguments plays the same role as in runPackage.

entries.name: list
entries.summary: The locked dependencies, then the programs Tey has installed. Outside a project there are no dependencies to show, so it is the programs alone rather than an error about a missing package.kex.

entries.name: buildSelected
signatures: buildSelected(packageName: String, workspace?: Bool, requestedJobs: String = …) -> Integer

entries.name: testReportingFlags
signatures: testReportingFlags(json?: Bool, list?: Bool, only: String) -> [String]
entries.summary:
How `tey test` should REPORT, as compiler flags (kexhq/kex#199).

`--json` and `--list` are for a tool reading the run rather than a person watching it: one JSON record per case, carrying the file and line of the `it` and of the failure, and — with `--list` — the cases discovered without any of them being run. `--only <name>` narrows the run to one case or one group.

Tey does not interpret any of it: the flags are the compiler's, the records are the compiler's, and this is the mapping from what a person typed to what the compiler is asked. Which is the point — an editor drives `tey test` because Tey knows the package's source roots, not because it wants Tey to reformat the answer (docs/testing.md).

entries.name: testSpecs
entries.summary: The spec files to run: the ones named on the line, or every `spec/*.spec.kex` when none were. Naming one is what an editor's per-file ▶ needs — and what anyone debugging a single suite in a package with thirty of them wants.

entries.name: test
signatures: test(requested: [String], interpret?: Bool, json?: Bool, list?: Bool, only: String) -> Integer

entries.name: testSelected

entries.name: new
entries.summary: `tey new <name>` — a package in a directory of its own, which the command creates. The pair with `init` below follows what `git init` and `cargo new` already taught everyone: `new` makes the directory, `init` adopts the one you are standing in.

entries.name: init
entries.summary:
`tey init` — a package in the CURRENT directory, named after it. This is the half that was missing: a repository someone had already made and cloned had no way to become a package except `tey new` in a temp directory and moving the files over by hand.

The name is overridable because a directory name is not always the package name — `kexhq/greet` checked out as `greet-main` is still `greet`.

remove(context: Context, name: String) -> Result<String, String>

entries.name: Tey.Lockfile
entries.summary: Pure, and declared so. Reading and writing `tey.lock` is somebody else's job — this module only turns the text into a LockState and back, which is what makes the whole format testable without a disk (tey/spec/lockfile.spec.kex).

entries.name: Command
entries.summary:
A project-specific command, run as `tey <name>`. Without these every package grows a Makefile or a bin/ script beside package.kex for "the way you run the linter", which the manifest — the one file a newcomer reads — says nothing about.

A name is one word, grouped with a colon: `db:migrate`, `assets:build`.

entries.name: Toolchain
entries.summary:
A toolchain package: the compiler executable plus the runtime and standard library it was built with, installed together so the three can never drift apart. Kex's own `package.kex` is the one that declares it — and a reader that did not know the declaration could not run any tey command from the compiler's own checkout, which is where it is most used.

Fields are prefixed like Command's: a bare `compiler` would be read as a method on an unpinned receiver before it is read as a field here.

entries.name: reservedCommands
entries.summary: The command names Tey answers itself. A `command(...)` may not take one of them: `tey test` must mean the same thing in every checkout, so a manifest that tries to redefine it is an error at read time rather than a silent shadow. Kept here because the READER is what enforces it, and Tey.Cli cannot be asked: it is built on this module, so reading the list off its declared commands would be a cycle. The two have to be kept in step by hand — one `.command(...)` in Tey.Cli, one name here (the first word is enough: `kex` covers every `kex ...` subcommand).

entries.name: read
entries.summary:
Reads a `package.kex`.

The compiler parses the manifest. Tey only interprets the resulting Kex AST, so comments, multiline calls, strings, and future grammar fixes cannot drift from the language that actually compiles package.kex.

entries.name: readWorkspace
entries.summary: Reads a virtual-workspace manifest: a package.kex whose root is `workspace` rather than a publishable package. Package-root workspaces are returned on ManifestPackage.manifestWorkspace by `read` above.

entries.name: Tey.Plugin
signatures: visibleBinding(bindings: [Binding], namespace: String, currentMember: String?) -> Result<Binding, String>
generator(binding: Binding, name: String) -> Result<PluginOperation, String>

entries.name: fingerprint
entries.summary: Fingerprints only the declared interface and requested resources. Provider implementation changes do not silently revoke approval; a capability, command schema, generator schema, or supported-Tey change does.

entries.name: validApprovals
entries.summary: Keeps only approvals still backed by an identical visible declaration. This is used when a lock is refreshed: removed plugins and interfaces whose resources changed cannot inherit an old authorization.

entries.name: visibleBinding
signatures: visibleBinding(bindings: [Binding], namespace: String, currentMember: String?) -> Result<Binding, String>

entries.name: generator
signatures: generator(binding: Binding, name: String) -> Result<PluginOperation, String>

entries.name: Tey.PluginHost
signatures: typedOptions(operation: Tey.Manifest.PluginOperation, supplied: {String: String}) -> Result<{String: Any}, String>

entries.name: encodeInvocation
entries.summary: The host-to-child half of protocol version 1. It is deliberately ordinary JSON rather than Kex source: a plugin receives data and cannot make Tey evaluate declarations smuggled into its context.

entries.name: typedOptions
signatures: typedOptions(operation: Tey.Manifest.PluginOperation, supplied: {String: String}) -> Result<{String: Any}, String>

entries.name: Tey.Programs
signatures: stage(root: String, destination: String) -> Result<Void, String>
copyInto(root: String, relative: String, destination: String) -> Bool
publishBuild(name: String, staged: String) -> Result<Void, String>
claim(target: String, packageName: String, receipts: [Receipt], exists?: Bool, teyBuilt?: Bool) -> Claim
refusal(target: String, claim: Claim, path: String, force?: Bool) -> String?
entries.summary:
What Tey has put in `${TEY_HOME}/bin`, and who owns each file there.

Every package whose targets Tey installs gets a receipt at `${TEY_HOME}/programs/<name>/receipt.json`. The receipt is the only authority for ownership: a file in the bin directory that no receipt lists is not Tey's to overwrite or delete. Without one, a second package declaring the same target name silently replaced the first package's program, and nothing could say what a file in there was or where it had come from.

Keyed by PACKAGE, not by binary: one package may install several targets, and reinstalling or removing it acts on all of them together.

entries.name: ProgramSource
entries.summary: What `tey install <argument>` names. `tey add` is how a dependency is added, so an argument to `tey install` always means a program.

entries.name: Claim
entries.summary: What installing one target name would do to the bin directory.

entries.name: reservedNames
entries.summary: Names that are Tey's own and never a package's to take: the `kex` shim lives in this directory, and replacing it would change which compiler every shell runs.

entries.name: classify
entries.summary: A path when it starts like one (`.`, `/`, `~`), a Git URL when it has a scheme or is scp-like (`git@host:owner/repo`), and otherwise the name of an installed program.

entries.name: buildDirectory
entries.summary: Where a program's staged build tree ends up once it is installed.

entries.name: stagingDirectory
entries.summary: A fresh directory to build a program in before it is installed. Beside `programs/` rather than in it, so a half-built tree is never listed as a program, and on the same filesystem, so publishing it is a rename.

entries.name: stage
signatures: stage(root: String, destination: String) -> Result<Void, String>
entries.summary: Copies the tree at `root` into `destination`: what a snapshot would hold, plus a committed `tey.lock` — the dependency versions the program's author tested, which a snapshot leaves out.

entries.name: copyInto
signatures: copyInto(root: String, relative: String, destination: String) -> Bool

entries.name: publishBuild
signatures: publishBuild(name: String, staged: String) -> Result<Void, String>
entries.summary: Replaces a program's build tree with the one it was just installed from. The old tree is moved aside first and removed last, so a failure part way leaves one of the two in place.

entries.name: claim
signatures: claim(target: String, packageName: String, receipts: [Receipt], exists?: Bool, teyBuilt?: Bool) -> Claim
entries.summary:
The decision for one target name, given every receipt and what is on disk. Pure, so the whole rule is testable without a bin directory.

`teyBuilt?` covers the programs a project-local `tey install` put here before receipts existed: they are escripts Tey itself wrote, so taking them into a receipt loses nothing, where refusing would make every existing installation demand `--force` on its next reinstall.

entries.name: refusal
signatures: refusal(target: String, claim: Claim, path: String, force?: Bool) -> String?
entries.summary: Why a claim stops the install, or None when it may go ahead. `--force` takes a name over from another package or from an unowned file, but never from Tey itself.

entries.name: all
entries.summary: Every receipt, by package name. An unreadable one is reported rather than skipped silently: skipping it would make the files it owns look unowned.

entries.name: save
entries.summary: Written beside the final file and renamed into place, so a reader never sees half a receipt and a failed write leaves the previous one intact.

entries.name: teyBuilt?
entries.summary: Whether `path` is an escript Tey's own target build wrote: its emulator line names `kex_main`, which every compiled Kex entry module is called.

entries.name: listLine
entries.summary: The line `tey list` prints for one installed program.

entries.name: Tey.Resolver
signatures: resolveWorkspaceWithInfo(context: Context, toolchain: Tey.Toolchain.ToolchainInfo) -> Result<LockState, String>

entries.name: resolveWorkspaceWithInfo
signatures: resolveWorkspaceWithInfo(context: Context, toolchain: Tey.Toolchain.ToolchainInfo) -> Result<LockState, String>
entries.summary: The caller may already have inspected the selected compiler while deciding whether an existing lock is reusable. Passing that result through keeps the `--info` contract to one invocation per install/resolve decision.

entries.name: UpgradeOutcome
entries.summary:
Upgrading Tey itself (`tey upgrade`), for installs that came from a release archive rather than a package manager — see `install.sh` at the repository root. A Homebrew-managed Tey is brew's to upgrade and is refused here.

Tey has its own version and its own cadence (`tey/package.kex`), so it cannot reuse the Kex tag list directly: the newest Tey is the one the newest Kex release's manifest declares. That manifest is read over plain HTTPS (raw.githubusercontent.com) with the same curl-then-wget idiom `Tey.Toolchain.download` already uses — no GitHub API, no rate limits, no clone. The archive itself is the `tey-<version>.tar.gz` the release workflow publishes beside the Kex archives, under the same tag.

What `tey upgrade` found: either the version it installed and where, or why there was nothing to install.

entries.name: currentPrefix
entries.summary: Where this Tey is installed, or None when it cannot be told — outside an installed launcher (a source checkout, `erl` by hand) there is nothing safe to overwrite. `tey/bin/tey` exports TEY_EBIN before invoking the BEAM, so a released install always knows.

entries.name: installEbin
entries.summary: The launcher's own runtime directory. TEY_EBIN can instead name the Tey paired with the selected Kex (see `installPaired`), which is not an install to upgrade — TEY_INSTALL_EBIN always names the launcher's.

entries.name: prefixOf
entries.summary: TEY_EBIN with the trailing `/lib/kex/tey/ebin` stripped. Anything else — unset, empty, a checkout's `tey/ebin` — is None: there is no install prefix to upgrade in place.

entries.name: homebrewManaged?
entries.summary: Whether this install belongs to Homebrew, whose keg bookkeeping Tey must not fight: that Tey upgrades with `brew upgrade tey`.

entries.name: manifestVersion
entries.summary: The `version("...")` line of a `package.kex` manifest, read as plain text. The manifest reader cannot be used here: it parses a LOCAL package through the selected compiler, and this text was just downloaded, not installed.

entries.name: compareVersions
entries.summary:
Ordering for two version strings, for the already-newest guard. Something unparsable compares as older: a hand-edited development version must never read as "newer than every release" and refuse its own upgrade.

Written over `newer?` rather than `compare` on purpose: a trait method from another module's `make ..., implement: Comparable` does not dispatch to a custom record from outside that module on the BEAM backend, while a plain `let` like `newer?` calls anywhere.

entries.name: carryBakedErlText
entries.summary: A source install (`make -C tey install`) bakes an absolute `erl` into `bin/tey`; release archives bake a bare `erl` resolved from PATH. Upgrading must not silently move the former onto the latter, so the old absolute path is carried into the new launcher. Anything else (no line, a relative `erl`, the dev placeholder) leaves the new launcher exactly as published.

entries.name: tagFor
entries.summary: The tag naming a Kex version, resolved against a tag list read once — `Tey.Toolchain.releaseTag` answers the same question but re-lists the tags on every call, which a pinned-version scan cannot afford.

entries.name: upgradeLatest
entries.summary: `tey upgrade` — the newest released Tey: the one the newest Kex release's manifest declares. Stable Kex releases unless `includePre` (`--pre`), which is how a pre-release Tey is reached without knowing its number.

entries.name: upgradePinned
entries.summary: `tey upgrade <version>` — exactly that Tey, from the newest release (stable first, then pre-releases) whose manifest declares it. An older version is allowed: pinning is explicit, and it is the way back from a bad release.

entries.name: installPaired
entries.summary:
The Tey a Kex release ships, unpacked beside that toolchain so `bin/tey` runs it whenever that Kex is selected: Kex and Tey are developed and released as a pair, and a pre-release is only tested properly as that pair. Nothing installed is replaced — not even a Homebrew keg — which is what makes this safe to do on every `tey kex install`.

The answer is the Tey version unpacked, or None when it was already there: tags do not move, so neither does what they carry.

entries.name: SemanticVersion
entries.summary: SemanticVersion is Comparable, so `a.compare(b)` answers Less/Equal/Greater like every other ordered type in the stdlib, and ordering reads as an ordering rather than as sign arithmetic on -1/0/1.

entries.name: release
entries.summary: The release a version belongs to: `0.4.0-rc.1` → `0.4.0`. Used where a pre-release should count as its eventual release.

entries.name: stable?
entries.summary: Whether a version is a full release rather than a pre-release. This is the question a download page asks: "what is the current stable Kex?".

entries.name: intersect
entries.summary:
The requirement satisfied only by versions satisfying BOTH, for when two packages in one graph each ask for the same dependency.

Concatenation, because `satisfies` already reads a requirement as a list of space-separated clauses that must ALL hold: `~> 0.1` and `>= 0.1.5` intersect to `~> 0.1 >= 0.1.5`, which is exactly the question "satisfies both". No interval arithmetic, no second implementation of the operators to keep in step with the first.

An empty intersection is not detected here, and deliberately: `~> 0.1 ~> 0.2` is perfectly well formed and simply matches nothing. Emptiness is a fact about the versions a repository actually publishes, so it is discovered where the tags are (`highest`), where the error can also say what WAS available.

entries.name: intersectAll
entries.summary: Every constraint at once. `[]` and `[""]` both mean "no opinion", which is what a package with no version requirement expresses.

entries.name: versionOf
entries.summary: The version inside a resolved ref: `refs/tags/v0.1.1` and `v0.1.1` both give `0.1.1`. A ref that carries no version (a branch name, a bare commit) gives "", which satisfies nothing and so never claims to meet a range.

entries.name: channelRank
entries.summary: Channel precedence, lowest first: prealpha < alpha < beta < rc < release. Plain semver would order these alphabetically — putting `beta` BEFORE `prealpha` — which is not what the words mean, so the ranking is explicit.

entries.name: range?
entries.summary: Whether a requested tag is a RANGE rather than one exact tag. `v1.2.0` is a name to look up; `~> 1.2` is a question to answer against everything the repository has.

entries.name: newer?
entries.summary: Descending semantic order, for picking the newest of anything. A tag that is not a version sorts after every tag that is, so a stray `nightly` can never displace a release.

entries.name: highest
entries.summary: The highest tag that satisfies the requirement — the whole point of writing a range instead of a version. None when nothing does.

entries.name: Tey.Snapshot
signatures: create(name: String, declaredPath: String, declaringRoot: String) -> Result<Tey.Lockfile.Dependency, String>

entries.name: create
signatures: create(name: String, declaredPath: String, declaringRoot: String) -> Result<Tey.Lockfile.Dependency, String>
entries.summary: Turns a path dependency into an immutable, content-addressed cache entry. The declared path remains in the lockfile for explanation; builds use the snapshot identified by `sha256`, never the live directory.

entries.name: sourceFiles
entries.summary: The files a snapshot of `root` holds, relative to it: everything but VCS metadata, build output and `.teyignore` matches.

entries.name: contentDigest
entries.summary: The content digest a snapshot of `root` is published under.

entries.name: Tey.Toolchain
signatures: installSource(source: String, version: String) -> Result<String, String>
download(url: String, path: String) -> Result<Void, String>
verifyArchive(archive: String, checksumUrl: String) -> Result<Void, String>
publish(staging: String, prefix: String) -> Result<String, String>

entries.name: ToolchainInfo
entries.summary: Facts reported by the compiler Tey selected for this project. This is deliberately not Kex.VERSION: that names the compiler which built Tey itself, and a package may select a newer (or older) compiler to build its own sources.

entries.name: repository
entries.summary: Where `tey kex list` looks for releases. Overridable so a fork or a mirror can be used without patching Tey.

entries.name: binDirectory
entries.summary: The directory holding the `kex` shim. It is what a user puts on PATH once; selecting a version repoints the shim rather than asking them to edit PATH again.

entries.name: selected
entries.summary: The version `tey kex use` last selected, if any.

entries.name: installedVersions
entries.summary: Versions installed under this Tey home, newest first. Staging leftovers are not installations, and neither is a directory whose `bin/kex` is gone — a half-removed toolchain must not be offered as one somebody can run.

entries.name: binaryOf
entries.summary: The `bin/kex` naming an installed version — the toolchain layout every consumer (the shim, `resolved`, the listings) agrees on, in one place.

entries.name: pairedTeyEbin
entries.summary: Where the Tey released with a Kex version lives — `bin/tey` reads the same path. Beside the toolchain rather than inside it: reinstalling a Kex replaces its whole directory, and a Tey running from there would lose its modules mid-run.

entries.name: availableVersions
entries.summary: Released versions, newest first, read from the repository's tags. Tags that are not versions are skipped rather than reported as junk.

entries.name: latestStable
entries.summary: The newest RELEASED version — what `tey kex install` picks when asked for no version in particular, and what a download page means by "the current Kex". Pre-releases are opt-in by name.

entries.name: latestIncludingPreReleases
entries.summary: The newest version of ANY channel — what `tey kex install --pre` picks. This is how you get onto a beta or an rc without knowing its number: during a pre-stability run there may be nothing else published at all.

entries.name: bundled
entries.summary: The Kex bundled beside Tey — what a package manager lays down so the first `tey` command has a compiler without a ten-minute build. It is a SEED, not an installation: `kex` below adopts it into the Tey home on first use, and from then on Tey manages that copy like any other version. Nothing outside the Tey home is ever put on PATH, which is the whole point — two `kex` binaries under two managers drift apart.

entries.name: bundledVersion
entries.summary: Which version the bundled Kex is. Answering means RUNNING it, so this is not something to ask inside a loop — but it is the only way to know: the seed is a plain install tree with no version recorded beside it.

entries.name: Toolchain
entries.summary: One selectable Kex: the version `tey kex use` names it by, the binary that runs it, and whether it is the bundled seed lying beside Tey rather than an installation in the Tey home.

entries.name: selectableToolchains
entries.summary:
Every version `tey kex use` can select, newest first: the ones in the Tey home, plus the bundled one — each carrying the binary that runs it, which is what a listing meant for tools (`kex list --installed --json`) needs.

The seed belongs here even though it is not installed. It is a real compiler already on the disk, and on a fresh keg it is the one a bare `kex` runs — so leaving it out made `tey kex use <that version>` refuse a version the user had just watched run, with no way back to it short of downloading a second copy of what was already there.

entries.name: selectableVersions
entries.summary: Every version `tey kex use` can select, newest first.

entries.name: resolveSelector
entries.summary:
Turns what someone typed after `tey kex use` into a version number.

`latest` means the newest Kex this machine can select — NOT the newest released one. `use` selects among what is already here; reaching for something unreleased-and-undownloaded is what `tey kex install` is for, and quietly downloading from a command that reads like "switch to" would be a surprise.

entries.name: kex
entries.summary:
The compiler every Tey command shells out to.

In order: an explicit TEY_KEX, the selected toolchain, the bundled seed (adopted on the spot), and only then a bare `kex` from PATH. That last one is a fallback for a source checkout, not a supported installation — a `kex` somebody else installed is a `kex` Tey cannot update, and it silently becomes a different version from the one `tey kex list` reports.

entries.name: activeInfo
entries.summary: Read the machine contract from the selected compiler. Keeping this in one call prevents dependency resolution and OTP validation from accidentally observing two different binaries if selection changes between them.

entries.name: runtimeOtpFloor
entries.summary:
The OTP release that compiled the selected toolchain's runtime beams — the oldest Erlang that can load them, since a `.beam` cannot be read by a runtime older than the `erlc` that produced it.

Read from `kex --info` rather than guessed: the number is a build-time constant inside the binary (KEX_RUNTIME_OTP_FLOOR) and Tey has no other way to see it. `--version` is prose and may be reworded; `--info` is the contract (tests/info_cli_test.cxx pins it).

`None` when the toolchain is too old to have `--info`, when the field is absent, or when it is `null` because the compiler was built without erlc. All three mean the same thing to a caller — "this toolchain does not say" — and none of them is an error worth stopping a build for.

entries.name: runningOtpRelease
entries.summary: The OTP actually about to run, asked of `erl` itself.

entries.name: erl
entries.summary: The `erl` Tey and Kex will spawn. KEX_ERL mirrors what the compiler itself honours, so overriding it moves both rather than half of the pair.

entries.name: resolved
entries.summary:
The compiler Tey would run, or None when there is none to run.

The bundled Kex is used WHERE IT LIES rather than copied into the Tey home first. Copying is an install, and an install is not something to do behind someone's back on their first command — it is also impossible where it would be most useful, since Homebrew's post-install sandbox cannot write to the user's home at all. So a fresh Homebrew keg is runnable immediately, nothing is written until `tey kex install` is typed, and a selected version always wins over the bundled one.

Without the last-resort fallback to a bare `kex` from PATH that `kex` above keeps: `kex` on PATH is Tey's own dispatcher, and answering it with its own name would send it round in a circle.

entries.name: installBundled
entries.summary: Takes the bundled Kex into the Tey home so Tey manages it like any other version: `tey kex list` shows it, `tey kex use` can come back to it, and uninstalling whatever replaces it leaves something behind. Only ever done when asked — see `resolved`.

entries.name: selectionHealthy?
entries.summary: Whether the selected toolchain is actually there. A `current` naming a version somebody deleted leaves every command failing on a path that does not exist, which reads like a broken Tey rather than a missing Kex.

entries.name: installRelease
entries.summary:
Installs a released version by name. The published archive for this machine is the fast path — unpacking one takes seconds where building takes minutes, and it needs no compiler, which is the point: whatever installs Tey should not also have to be able to build Kex.

Falling back to a source build rather than failing keeps the platforms without a published archive working, and covers a release whose upload is incomplete.

entries.name: ArchiveFailure
entries.summary: Why a published archive could not be installed. The distinction is the point: one of these is routine and one of them is not.

entries.name: releaseBase
entries.summary: Where the release archives live. Derived from the repository so a fork only has to set TEY_KEX_REPO, and overridable on its own for a mirror.

entries.name: releaseTarget
entries.summary: The archive naming this machine, matching what the release workflow builds: `kex-0.4.0-macos-arm64.tar.gz`.

entries.name: installSource
signatures: installSource(source: String, version: String) -> Result<String, String>
entries.summary: Installs compiler, runtime BEAM modules and stdlib sources together. The source tree's CMake install layout is the toolchain ABI Tey manages.

entries.name: uninstall
entries.summary: Removes an installed toolchain. Refuses to leave the shim pointing at nothing: removing the SELECTED version also clears the selection, and the caller is told to pick another.

entries.name: download
signatures: download(url: String, path: String) -> Result<Void, String>
entries.summary:
The archive download/verify/hash/tag/publish helpers below are public because `Tey.SelfUpdate` (`tey upgrade`) reuses the exact same release mechanics for Tey's own archives that Kex toolchains already trust — same URLs, same checksums, same staged swaps. No behavior change; only visibility.

curl, then wget: one of the two is on essentially every machine that can reach a release, and this way Tey needs neither an HTTP library nor a compiler to fetch one.

entries.name: verifyArchive
signatures: verifyArchive(archive: String, checksumUrl: String) -> Result<Void, String>
entries.summary: The published `.sha256` is `<hash>  <filename>`, the format both sha256sum and shasum write and read.

entries.name: checksumOf
entries.summary: Hashed with an external tool rather than read in: the archive is tens of megabytes of binary, and this keeps all of it out of the process.

entries.name: releaseTag
entries.summary: The tag naming this version in the repository — `0.3.0` or `v0.3.0`.

entries.name: versionOf
entries.summary: `v0.3.0` → Just("0.3.0"). A tag that is not a version is None, which `collect` drops: a toolchain is named by its version, not by a label.

entries.name: publish
signatures: publish(staging: String, prefix: String) -> Result<String, String>
entries.summary: Swaps a finished staging tree in for `prefix`. A reinstall keeps the old tree until the new one is in place and puts it back if the move fails, so a failed upgrade leaves the previous toolchain working rather than none.

entries.name: Tey.Version
entries.summary: GENERATED by tey/Makefile from tey/package.kex — do not edit.

entries.name: number
entries.summary: Tey's own version, as declared by package.kex's version(...) line.

entries.name: Tey.Workspace
signatures: select(context: Context, packageName: String, workspace?: Bool) -> Result<[Member], String>

entries.name: discover
entries.summary: Discovers the outermost workspace containing `start`. Without a workspace, the nearest package is a one-member context. Paths are lexical and absolute; discovery never changes the process working directory.

entries.name: select
signatures: select(context: Context, packageName: String, workspace?: Bool) -> Result<[Member], String>
entries.summary: Selects the members a workspace-aware command should operate on. An explicit package always wins; otherwise commands at a member stay local, while commands at the workspace root (or another non-member directory) use every member. `--workspace` broadens the implicit member selection.

entries.name: dependencyLayers
entries.summary: Dependency-ready layers for workspace-wide commands. Cyclic leftovers form one final layer so callers can continue, while discovery reports the cycle.

entries.name: options
entries.summary: A function rather than a module-level constant: on BEAM, calling a make-method (`.parse`, `.help`) on a module-level constant fails with "Undefined function" — the dispatcher doesn't resolve the constant.

entries.name: Tey.Docgen.Extract
signatures: pageFor(source: String, items: [Kex.AST.Node], header: String) -> SourcePage
constantFromPending(p: Pending, info: Kex.AST.FunctionInfo, prefix: String) -> Pending
addClause(p: Pending, info: Kex.AST.FunctionInfo, lists: [[ParamSig]]) -> Pending
indexedFind(accum: [Pending], name: String, index: Integer) -> Integer?
docNamedSignature(name: String, ref: Kex.AST.TypeRef, doc: Doc) -> String
paramText(name: String, typeName: String, hasDefault: Bool) -> String
displayName(p: ParamSig, index: Integer, doc: Doc) -> String
withPeerType(p: ParamSig, index: Integer, peers: [[ParamSig]]) -> ParamSig

entries.name: pageFor
signatures: pageFor(source: String, items: [Kex.AST.Node], header: String) -> SourcePage
entries.summary: `header` is the file's opening comment when a blank line separates it from what follows (Index.fileHeader). The AST reader attaches every comment above a declaration to it, blank lines and all, so the first declaration's doc arrives with the file's introduction glued on top — algebra.kex's "Algebraic structures: ..." read as the summary of `Monoid`. The header is cut off that doc here and kept as the page's own intro.

entries.name: detachHeader
entries.summary: The items with the header removed from the first documented one.

entries.name: pageTitle
entries.summary: A page's title is the declaration it is really about — "OptionParser", not the file name's "Optionparser", and "FileHandle", not "Filehandle". Preference order: a single top-level module, then a single top-level type/record/trait, then the file name title-cased.

entries.name: baseSpelling
entries.summary: "FileHandle<CanRead, W>" -> "FileHandle", "FS.Path" -> "Path": what the file could plausibly be named after.

entries.name: moduleTitle
entries.summary: The title of a file with one top-level module. The file's stem has a say when the module is shared across several files: data/queue.kex declares `module Data` around `module Queue`, and so do set.kex and stack.kex — without the stem, every one of those pages is titled "Data" and the sidebar shows indistinguishable entries. A module whose last segment matches the stem is the page ("dns.kex" -> Net.DNS); else a nested module matching it is ("queue.kex" -> Data.Queue); else the top module stands ("mock.kex" -> Mock, a file about the family).

entries.name: fileStem
entries.summary: "kex/ast" -> "ast".

entries.name: Pending
entries.summary: Accumulator entries: finished entities or functions still collecting.

entries.name: ParamSig
entries.summary: One parameter as a clause declares it. `named` is false for a pattern parameter (`let repeat(0) = ...`), whose spelling is a value, not a name a signature should show.

entries.name: mergeMakes
entries.summary: Two `make Queue<A>` blocks in one file (one for the collection traits, one for Blankable) are one set of methods to a reader: the later block folds into the first, traits and members appended.

entries.name: variantEntry
entries.summary: A named helper (rather than an inline lambda) so the element type of `v.fields` comes from VariantInfo, not from VariantEntry's [String].

entries.name: isConstantBinding
entries.summary: A binding with no parameter list is a constant — unless it is `foul`, in which case it is a zero-argument FUNCTION that Kex auto-calls. `IO.out` is a handle that is always the same one; `IO.getLine` reads a new line every time it is named, and calling that a constant is a lie about both what it does and when it happens.

entries.name: constantFromPending
signatures: constantFromPending(p: Pending, info: Kex.AST.FunctionInfo, prefix: String) -> Pending
entries.summary: The annotation arrived first and created a PendingFunction; the binding now replaces it with the constant entry, keeping name/doc/line.

entries.name: addClause
signatures: addClause(p: Pending, info: Kex.AST.FunctionInfo, lists: [[ParamSig]]) -> Pending

entries.name: indexedFind
signatures: indexedFind(accum: [Pending], name: String, index: Integer) -> Integer?

entries.name: declaredReturn
entries.summary: The one return type the source commits to: the annotation's result, or the inline `-> T` of an unannotated clause. What the @return tag says is checked against this (Index.reportDocDrift), never shown instead of it.

entries.name: finalResult
entries.summary: What a curried type finally answers: `A -> (A -> T -> A) -> A` is A.

entries.name: functionTypes
entries.summary: The type names a function is about — every parameter type plus the result type of each annotation, deduplicated. This is what lets search answer "what touches Integer" rather than just "what is called Integer".

entries.name: signatureTexts
entries.summary: A signature names every parameter WITH its type and ends in the result: `and(a: Integer, b: Integer) -> Integer`. The names come from a clause, the types from the annotation (flattened to the clause's arity), from the clause's own inline annotations, or — for a method nobody annotated — from its @param/@return tags. A zero-parameter member reads as the property it looks like at the call site (`sum : Number`). A method with no clause at all (a trait's required method) has only its type, and borrows parameter names from its @param tags when they line up.

entries.name: plainSignature
entries.summary: A signature built from the clause alone: inline types first, the doc tags as the fallback, bare names when neither says.

entries.name: docNamedSignature
signatures: docNamedSignature(name: String, ref: Kex.AST.TypeRef, doc: Doc) -> String
entries.summary: An annotation with no clause to take names from: the @param tags name the parameters when there are exactly as many as the type has.

entries.name: paramText
signatures: paramText(name: String, typeName: String, hasDefault: Bool) -> String

entries.name: parenthesized
entries.summary: A function type inside a parameter list reads as the parameter's type only in parentheses: `f: (T -> Void)`, not `f: T -> Void`.

entries.name: displayName
signatures: displayName(p: ParamSig, index: Integer, doc: Doc) -> String
entries.summary: A pattern parameter (`repeat(0)`) shows the name its @param tag gives that position, or `_` — never the literal, which reads as an argument.

entries.name: bestParams
entries.summary: Of several clauses' parameter lists, the one that names the most parameters — `repeat(n: Integer)` over `repeat(0)` — merged with the types the other clauses of the same arity declare.

entries.name: withPeerType
signatures: withPeerType(p: ParamSig, index: Integer, peers: [[ParamSig]]) -> ParamSig

entries.name: signatureTypeText
entries.summary: Source-style type text: function arrows chain to the right without the redundant parentheses typeRefText adds, and a function-typed parameter is parenthesized so `(X -> Y) -> Z` stays distinct from `X -> Y -> Z`.

entries.name: flattenToArity
entries.summary: Absorbs single-parameter curried layers while more than one argument remains. `(FilePath) -> (Read) -> R` with arity 2 becomes `(FilePath, Read) -> R`.

entries.name: clauseParams
entries.summary: `type` is a keyword after `.`, so typed-record access goes through pattern matching instead.

entries.name: qualify
entries.summary: Modules may be written fully qualified (`module FS.File do` inside `module FS do`), so a dotted name already carries its prefix — never prepend twice. A short name gets the parent's prefix as usual.

signatures: unitData(model: PackageModel, source: String, toc: [TocEntry]) -> Any
entries.summary: Everything a theme might show beside the body: which unit and version this is (the header badge), where the source lives, and the page's sections for an "On this page" list.

entries.name: tocHtml
entries.summary: The rail as markup too, so a theme template can place it without walking JSON: a template language that sees the data as `Any` cannot iterate it. A page with a single section has nothing to navigate.

entries.name: unitRoot
entries.summary: "/prelude/0.4.0/": where the unit is mounted.

entries.name: navTree
entries.summary: The page tree, nested the way the standalone sidebar nests it: a module family (Net, Net.DNS, Net.HTTP) is one branch.

entries.name: navNode
signatures: navNode(page: SourcePage, pages: [SourcePage], model: PackageModel) -> Any

entries.name: tocOf
entries.summary: The sections a reader can jump to, in page order: each declaration with a section of its own, and those a module declares.

entries.name: descriptionOf
entries.summary: One sentence for the page's <meta name="description">: the file's intro, else what its first declaration says, else its title.

entries.name: absolutize
signatures: absolutize(html: String, model: PackageModel, urlPath: String) -> String
entries.summary: Every relative href in a fragment, rewritten to a site path: from the page at `urlPath`, "../net.html#module-net" is "/prelude/0.4.0/net/#module-net" and "index.html" is "/prelude/0.4.0/". A fragment-only href ("#x"), an absolute one and an external URL stay as they are.

entries.name: Tey.Docgen.Highlight
signatures: classifyWord(word: String, prevDot: Bool, nextCh: Char) -> String

entries.name: lexAll
entries.summary: out accumulates newest-first; the final reverse restores source order.

entries.name: lexString
entries.summary: cs starts after the opening quote; acc is newest-first tokens so far.

entries.name: takeStringText
entries.summary: Collect literal string text up to (not including) the closing quote, an interpolation opener, or the end of input. Backslash escapes are opaque.

entries.name: balancedBraces
entries.summary: From just after "${", collect the interpolation body up to its matching "}" (which is consumed but not collected). Embedded "..." strings are skipped whole so braces inside them do not count.

entries.name: skipString
entries.summary: Consume a whole "..." literal starting at the opening quote; returns the consumed characters (both quotes included) and the remainder.

entries.name: classifyWord
signatures: classifyWord(word: String, prevDot: Bool, nextCh: Char) -> String

entries.name: previousIsDot
entries.summary: The most recent token that is not whitespace: out is newest-first, so a plain find walks backwards in time.

entries.name: keywords
entries.summary: Functions rather than module constants: on BEAM, method calls on a module-level constant fail to dispatch.

entries.name: highlightLinked
entries.summary: The same highlighting, with every type name that `hrefOf` can place wrapped in a link to it — signatures read as code and navigate as a reference. `hrefOf` answers "" for a name it cannot place.

entries.name: esc
entries.summary: Local copy of Tey.Docgen.Html.esc — duplicating four replaces keeps the modules acyclic (Html calls Highlight for code blocks).
